entry.title: The Website Go-Live Checklist: 5 Critical Checks Beyond Good Looks
entry.summary: A website can look finished before it works. Anthony Dutcher of Vix Media Group shares a website go-live checklist for clear messaging, usable design and working inquiries.
entry.content:
A website can look finished before it works. Anthony Dutcher of Vix Media Group shares a website go-live checklist for clear messaging, usable design and working inquiries.

About the Author:
Anthony Dutcher is a Founding Partner at Vix Media Group, a Denver-based agency working across healthcare, technology, and media. His team is deliberately split between agency and in-house backgrounds and runs its own infrastructure, so it has sat on both sides of the brief. He believes research should drive design decisions.

A website can look finished before it is ready to use. The opening screen feels confident, the presentation goes well, and everyone agrees it looks better. Then somebody tries to find a specific service or send an inquiry from their phone. That moment is why every launch needs a website go-live checklist that goes beyond good looks.

That is the review I care about. At Vix Media Group, I want website development judged by what a visitor can understand and do, along with what a team can present.

In an October 16, 2026 project review, the report marked 31 of 32 requested changes complete. I still felt the work needed better judgment. The report told me which changes were done. It could not tell me whether the pages communicated well.

That distinction costs time if you discover it late. A completed checklist is useful, and judgment still has to sit on top of it. These five checks give the business owner and marketing team a practical review before sign-off. They complement the security, accessibility, and technical launch checks your web developers run.

1. Read the page as a customer would

Start with the question the visitor came to answer. Someone comparing services needs different information from someone who already knows what they want and needs to book.

For each important page, ask:

  • Can I tell what the business offers and who it is for?
  • Can I find the information I need to compare or trust it?
  • Do I understand what happens after I contact the business?

Read the sentences and headings. “Solutions designed around you” could belong to almost any company. “Interior design for offices, from layout planning to installation” gives a buyer something to work with.

Specific copy can still have personality. Good copy has a point of view and still answers the question. If the team has to explain the page over a call, put the missing explanation on the page.

2. Keep the character. Cut the friction.

Whitespace earns its place when it makes the page easier to read. It becomes waste when it makes the visitor work harder to connect the offer, the evidence, and the next step.

A headline does not need its own full screen just because it is short. A useful explanation shouldn’t become four separate sections just to fill a template. Before adding another block, ask what new question it answers.

On a phone, review the whole scroll. Keep a claim close to the information that supports it. Bring the next action into the same reading sequence. Remove repeated promises before shrinking type or hiding important details.

Length matters less than purpose. Aim for a page where every space does a job, and the information arrives when the reader needs it.

Make the business recognizable

A website should feel like the business behind it. I want confidence, a memorable image, and the moment that makes someone stop. The impressive part still needs to serve the page.

Strong branding can show up in a distinctive type treatment, a deliberate crop, or one well-chosen interaction. Not every section has to compete for attention.

Ask your web designers what would remain recognizable if you covered the logo. Then ask whether the same design still works when the visitor reads on a small screen, enlarges the text, or navigates without a mouse.

A beautiful movement that delays the answer is a tradeoff, so treat it as one. Keep the character and remove the obstacle.

3. Score the work, but do not let a score approve it

A useful score explains a decision. “Nine out of ten” does not help the team unless it says what is strong, what is weak, and what would change the verdict.

I would score these areas separately:

  • Clarity: can the intended customer understand the offer?
  • Character: does the design feel specific to this business?
  • Ease of use: can someone read, navigate, and act without confusion?

Agree on the scale before reviewing. One means the area fails its purpose. Five means it partly works but needs substantial correction. Ten means it meets the agreed brief, with no material weakness found in that review. A ten still makes no promise about commercial performance.

Pair every score with an observation and a next action. “The offer is clear, but the contact button disappears below a long empty section on mobile” is useful. “Needs more polish” is not.

Keep functional checks separate. A form either passed the specified test, failed it, or remains untested. Attractive typography cannot compensate for a lost inquiry. We approach launch readiness the same way: define what must work, who owns it, and what test proves it.

AI can help organize feedback or run a first review against agreed criteria. I would not treat its self-score as independent approval. Whether the first pass comes from software or a teammate, the person approving the work needs to inspect the result. An unchecked assumption stays unchecked, no matter how confidently it is scored.

4. Make feedback easy to locate and finish

Good feedback identifies the page, the problem, and the intended result. I use Tella for walkthroughs, and others on our team use Loom. Screen recordings let us show the reading sequence and point to exactly where something feels wrong.

The recording still needs to become actionable work. “Move this up” loses meaning once it is separated from the screen. Attach the relevant moment or image, name the section, and explain what the change should accomplish.

We have also built a way for clients to leave comments directly on our custom-built sites. The purpose is simple: keep feedback next to the work, so clients never have to describe a location in a long email.

For example, “Bring the contact action directly below the service explanation so I do not have to search for it” gives the team a concrete correction. Assign an owner, make the change, and return to the same page and screen size to check it. Record what was verified before closing the comment.

5. Test the path from interest to a real inquiry

Before approval, follow the route a customer would take. Open a service page, use the navigation, complete the form, and confirm that the inquiry reaches the intended destination. Check the confirmation message too: does the person know what happens next?

Ask the team to test failure cases as well as successful submission. What happens when a required field is empty, or the request cannot be sent? Can someone recover without starting over or wondering whether the message arrived?

Before launch, confirm that inquiry tracking distinguishes a button click from a submitted inquiry. After launch, use the available source data to see where inquiries come from. A well-reviewed page is a stronger starting point, and the market still has to respond.

Before you sign off

Ask the team for a simple record:

  1. The page and screen size checked.
  2. The issue found and the person responsible.
  3. What changed and the evidence that it worked.
  4. Anything still untested or awaiting approval.

I cannot put a defensible time-saving percentage on our newer feedback process yet. I would rather track review rounds, reopened issues, and problems found after approval than claim that a faster first draft made the whole project faster.

The standard is simple: the business is clear, the design has character, and the next step works. The review should leave the team knowing what changed and the owner knowing what they are approving.

Before you approve your next website, what can your team show you beyond a good-looking first screen?

entry.title: Space Is the New SaaS: 4 Lessons From Designing Websites for Aerospace Startups
entry.summary: Lunar hotels, orbital data centers, and satellite networks all need clear, credible sites. Flexy Global shares four lessons from designing websites for aerospace startups.
entry.content:
Lunar hotels, orbital data centers, and satellite networks all need clear, credible sites. Flexy Global shares four lessons from designing websites for aerospace startups.

About the Authors:
Garik Avetisyan, Davit Gabrielyan, and Anastasia Saroka are co-founders of Flexy Global, a design and development partner for startups and global enterprises. Garik built and successfully exited a consumer app used by millions. Davit brings 15 years of experience leading complex projects and operations at international companies including Orange and Coca-Cola Hellenic. Anastasia, Design Director at Flexy Global, brings experience designing products for large corporations and startups in the fitness industry. Together, they believe advanced technology creates greater value when people can understand it, trust it, and use it confidently.

Six years ago, when we founded Flexy Global, we chose a star for our logo. It represented the sense of magic we wanted to bring to our work: turning ambitious ideas into experiences that feel clear, thoughtful, and possible. Years later, that symbol took on a more literal meaning when we began designing websites for aerospace startups.

Today, we design websites for aerospace startups building lunar hotels, orbital AI data centers and space-based networks. Our work includes GRU Space, Starcloud and Exosat, along with several projects we cannot name yet.

Why aerospace startups need SaaS-grade websites

Across these projects, the recurring challenge has been the same. We have to make complex services clear, build trust in products that do not exist yet, and give the right audience a reason to act.

As the cost of sending payloads into space falls, the space economy could grow to the scale of national economies. Thousands of companies could offer new goods and services, from orbital computing to lunar bases. They will need the clarity, proof, and conversion paths of strong SaaS and e-commerce experiences.

Here are four lessons we have learned along the way.

1. Space is the new SaaS: sell what the rocket makes possible

Aerospace startups often lead with satellites, payloads, or engineering breakthroughs. Their customers want the outcomes those technologies enable.

Starcloud sells access to AI compute in orbit. Exosat offers satellite capacity and infrastructure to operators that need more control over their networks. GRU Space invites future guests to reserve a place in a lunar hotel. Each website needs to clarify the offer, identify its audience, and guide them to the next step.

For GRU, we treated the reservation path like luxury e-commerce with an unusually long sales cycle. The primary call to action stays visible throughout the experience. Meanwhile, the journey introduces the vision, the timeline, and the selective qualification process behind a stay planned for 2032.

Ambition still needs to lead to concrete action. Design for the wow, and make sure it ends in a conversion.

2. Design the gap between vision and proof

Aerospace startups often sell products scheduled to launch years from now, while investors, customers, and talent evaluate them today. That makes the roadmap central to the website story.

For Starcloud, the progression from Starcloud-1 to later missions shows how orbital computing can grow into commercial infrastructure. GRU follows a similar path, from lunar systems tests and habitat deployment to a hotel that can receive guests.

We brought these roadmaps into the main homepage journey. The scroll connects each long-term promise with the mission, milestone, or technical proof that moves it closer to reality. Visitors can follow the sequence and see how one stage prepares the next.

A timeline turns science fiction into a plan.

3. Proof beats renders

Renders help audiences understand products that are too large, too distant, or too early to photograph, and skilled 3D designers can make them convincing. Yet aerospace websites filled entirely with flawless satellites and glowing horizons can quickly feel speculative.

Starcloud-1 offers stronger proof. It launched in November 2025 carrying the first NVIDIA H100 GPU into orbit, later running Google’s Gemma model and training an AI model in space. Those achievements make the larger vision credible.

We grounded ambitious claims in real artifacts: hardware and mission photography, launch dates, named partners, technical milestones, and concrete firsts. The website keeps its sense of scale while giving visitors evidence they can verify.

Our practical rule is simple: one credible fact for every major render.

4. One site has to persuade four audiences

An aerospace website may need to address investors, customers, engineering talent, and press or regulators within the same experience. Each group arrives with different questions, so the content needs clear layers.

For Exosat, the first layer communicates the larger proposition: satellite infrastructure that gives sovereign operators more control. The next layer explains direct-to-device capability, compatibility with existing infrastructure, and faster coverage expansion. Deeper sections cover spectrum, orbit, latency, capacity, and manufacturing details for technical readers.

Across these projects, the headline establishes the strategic idea. The next sections explain customer value, and dedicated pages or deeper content provide the technical substance. Careers also get a clear route, because hiring is a major conversion for deep-tech startups.

The result is a focused experience that serves different levels of expertise. One story should offer several levels of detail.

The shared problem behind every aerospace website

GRU Space, Starcloud and Exosat operate in very different parts of the aerospace economy. Their websites still solve a shared communication problem. Each must turn a complex, future-facing idea into a service people can understand, trust, and act on today. For web designers entering the sector, that is the brief worth preparing for.

SpaceX’s push toward reusable launch systems has helped open the door to a new space economy. Orbital infrastructure, lunar settlements, and eventually asteroid resources could expand what humanity can build.

Elon Musk captures that future simply: “You want to wake up in the morning and think the future is going to be great.” The growing number of space startups is making that optimism feel tangible.

entry.title: Cross-Platform Design: Working Across Apple and Google Without Losing Your Point of View
entry.summary: Apple and Google each have strong design opinions. Nicolas Solerieu of Expo shares cross-platform design principles that respect both platforms while keeping your product recognizable.
entry.content:
Apple and Google each have strong design opinions. Nicolas Solerieu of Expo shares cross-platform design principles that respect both platforms while keeping your product recognizable.

About the Author:
Nicolas Solerieu is a product and brand designer at Expo, working across product, web, and brand identity. Previously at GitHub and Opendoor, he’s interested in software, the web, and the strange craft of arranging rectangles for a living.

Apple and Google have become increasingly opinionated about expressive design, making cross-platform design a fun, hot topic. It is also hard to navigate, given how many form factors and platforms exist today. Apple’s Liquid Glass leans into translucency, depth, and fluidity. Google’s Material 3 Expressive favors bold shapes, colors, typography, and springy motion. Both are compelling, and each has its own personality. Neither is guaranteed to suit your brand.

That creates an interesting dilemma when you design one product for both ecosystems, and beyond.

Cross-platform development has long promised parity: one codebase, one design system, and ideally the same experience everywhere. The efficiency makes sense. A consistent product still doesn’t need to look identical on every platform, and making everything match can become a strange priority. None of your users compare screenshots. They’re just trying to use the thing.

Know the rules before breaking them

Designing for multiple platforms requires some familiarity with each ecosystem. App designers working across both should:

  • Understand device constraints, safe areas, and system UI.
  • Follow established navigation and interaction patterns.
  • Know when to use native components and controls.
  • Use both platforms regularly, particularly their default apps.

That last one is where the gold is.

You can learn the guidelines and UI kits. Knowing how something should work still doesn’t tell you how it should feel. That’s where design judgment, or taste, comes in.

Opening a menu, dismissing a sheet, going back a screen: ordinary stuff, until something feels slightly off. Timing, gestures, and transitions are difficult to appreciate in a Figma file. Spending time on both platforms helps you notice the expectations you’ve stopped noticing on your own phone.

The documentation is extensive. The examples are in our pockets. We might as well use them.

Decide what makes it yours

Before deciding what should change between platforms, establish what should stay consistent.

Your product’s identity might come from its typography, illustration, writing, or information hierarchy. Perhaps it’s a particular interaction or the physical product itself. Perhaps the content does most of the work, and the interface can stay quiet.

Consider a space travel app. I’m using a concept here, so we can conveniently skip the engineering complications of getting to Mars.

Large planetary imagery, spacecraft, deep black backgrounds, and compact flight information establish its visual world. Those qualities can carry across platforms even if the menus and navigation differ. The spacecraft looks cool, but at its core, this is an airline UX with booking, boarding, and onboard experiences.

The useful question is what people would recognize as yours. A particular corner radius probably won’t carry the whole brand, and neither will translucency.

A checklist for the native-versus-custom debate

You don’t have to choose between fully native and fully custom. I’d argue that deciding for an entire app is usually the wrong approach.

Judge it at the component level. Here are a few questions worth bringing into a design review:

  • What does the user already know? Preserve familiar navigation, gestures, and controls unless changing them offers a clear benefit. Learning your app shouldn’t require them to unlearn their phone.
  • What does customization contribute? A clearer visualization? A better interaction? Some personality? All valid reasons. “We wanted our own button” needs a little more explanation.
  • What should stay consistent? Identify the language, information hierarchy, and visual qualities that define the product. Give the team something concrete to preserve.
  • Have we tried the whole flow on both devices? Include the keyboard, menus, transitions, and system UI. Two tidy screenshots can hide two very different experiences.
  • Does it survive ordinary complications? Larger text, long names, reduced motion, screen readers, loading, and errors. The flattering mockup is only one state.
  • Can we maintain it? Involve app developers early and document intentional differences. A clever variation becomes less charming when nobody remembers why it exists.

These questions won’t make the decision for you. They should make the discussion more useful.

Put it to work: a flight to Mars

In the space travel concept, browsing destinations is a good place to build something custom. Large views of Mars and the Moon make exploration part of the experience. A shared layout gives unfamiliar information, such as gravity, transit time, and available bases, a predictable structure.

The imagery provides the spectacle. The hierarchy helps people compare. Both are worth preserving across platforms.

The boarding pass calls for a different balance. The spacecraft image gives it personality, but departure time, boarding status, seat, and barcode still need to be immediately readable. A beautiful ship won’t help someone find their gate. A boarding pass is a familiar pattern that doesn’t need reinventing.

This is where the checklist becomes practical. What happens with a longer passenger name? Larger text? A delayed departure? Those states should influence the layout before we get too attached to it.

The flight tracker offers another chance to create a signature experience. A spacecraft above a planet gives the journey scale, while progress and telemetry communicate its status. That visualization could remain consistent across platforms, with motion respecting accessibility preferences.

Around these moments, passenger selection, sharing and routine menus can follow platform conventions. There’s plenty of room for personality without redesigning every supporting control.

Flexibility has a cost

Some products benefit from leaning heavily into their operating system. Utility apps often gain more from familiarity and efficiency than from an elaborate visual identity.

Others, like Duolingo, have built a recognizable world of their own. Their personality is part of the experience. Most products sit somewhere in between.

There’s work involved either way. Platform differences need designing and testing. Custom controls need accessibility and interaction details that standard components may already handle.

For a small team, sharing most of the interface can be a perfectly reasonable choice. Spend the extra effort where you can explain what it improves. You don’t need a philosophical commitment to either extreme.

Let the technology follow

Frameworks like Expo make this approach practical. With Expo UI, developers can use native SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose components alongside custom React Native interfaces. For the space travel concept, that could mean native booking controls alongside a custom planet browser and flight tracker. The implementation follows the role of each component.

The native-versus-React-Native debate often treats cross-platform as a compromise you make until you can afford something better. From a design and brand perspective, I find that framing pretty limiting. A shared interface can be a deliberate choice. Your product has its own point of view, and preserving it across devices is a perfectly good ambition.

AI makes this even more interesting. Agentic workflows and simulators make it easier to generate separate implementations. Keeping them coherent, testing them, and refining the details still takes work. More code isn’t automatically more progress. I’d rather spend that effort improving the experience than maintaining differences nobody asked for.

That’s why React Native and other cross-platform frameworks appeal to me as a designer. They give small teams room to build a recognizable product, share the work that benefits from consistency, and adapt where the platform calls for it. That flexibility serves both the brand and the reality of building something.

Respect the platform. Apple and Google already have art directors. Your product needs one too.

 ⁠

entry.title: The Interface Is Disappearing: What Designers Actually Design in the Age of AI Agents
entry.summary: As agents take over workflows, designers spend less time on screens. Unfold on product design in the age of AI agents, and when an interface is still needed.
entry.content:
As agents take over workflows, designers spend less time on screens. Unfold on product design in the age of AI agents, and when an interface is still needed.

About the Author: 
Unfold Founder & Creative Director Eddie Lobanovskiy builds high-impact brand identities and UI/UX ecosystems at the intersection of classical design and AI innovation. Designer of the XRP logo.

For most of the history of software, design meant screens. People clicked through dashboards, opened menus, and moved between apps to get one job done. That pattern is changing. More and more, people tell an agent what they want done, and the agent works across tools in the background. Design in the age of AI agents starts from that shift.

It changes what designers actually design. We still design screens, though fewer of them. Increasingly, we design behaviors, instructions, permissions, handoffs, states, and the moment an agent takes action.

At Unfold, we see this in our own work. A growing share of our recent projects involve agents, connectors, skills, plugins, and workflows, where a few years ago we would have built standalone app screens. Here is what that shift has taught us so far.

From clicking through tools to telling an agent what to do

We have already started replacing standalone tools with agents. A workflow that used to mean opening several apps can now run as one request. The agent moves through the steps across those tools while the person does something else.

Think of a weekly client report. Traditionally, someone pulls numbers from an analytics tool, updates a project board, drafts a summary, and sends it. An agent can handle each step. The person’s job moves from operating the tools to stating the goal and checking the result.

For designers, the starting question changes. We used to ask which screen a user needs next. Now we often ask what the user is trying to get done, and how much of it they want to watch happen.

Intent, action, result: the new shape of UX

Traditional software might require five screens and ten clicks to complete a task. An agent experience may need only three moments: a prompt, a confirmation, and a result.

We think of the new UX as intent, action, and result, and each stage carries its own design problems. Intent needs to be captured clearly, even when the request is vague. Action needs boundaries, so the agent knows what it may do alone and what needs approval. The result needs to be presented so the person can trust it, check it, and change it.

Fewer screens still leave plenty to design. The decisions move from layout into logic, language, and timing.

Apps become infrastructure, agents become the interface

People will keep using CRMs, project management platforms and analytics software. What changes is how they reach them. The agent increasingly becomes the layer people interact with, and the apps sit underneath as infrastructure.

That raises new questions for product teams. If users rarely open your product directly, where does your brand live? How do people know which system did what? What happens when an agent pulls data from one tool and writes it into another? These are as much design questions as engineering ones.

What we design now: behaviors, permissions and handoffs

Our recent work has shifted toward agents, connectors, skills, plugins, and workflows, often designed as clusters of capabilities. Our product design work now regularly includes deliverables that never appear on a screen.

We define how an agent should behave when a request is ambiguous. We decide which actions it can take on its own and which need a person’s approval. We map handoffs between agents, tools, and people, and the states a task can move through along the way. We also write the instructions that shape how the agent responds.

Good design here means making AI feel predictable, trustworthy, understandable, and easy to control. A polished interface still matters, but it cannot make up for an agent whose behavior surprises people.

Designing confirmation and transparency

Confirmation and transparency have become central UX problems in our work. If an agent is about to send a message, change data, spend money, or interact with another system, the person needs to understand what will happen before it happens.

A useful confirmation shows the action, the target, and the consequence in plain language. “Send this proposal to three client contacts” tells the person exactly what they are approving. A bare “Proceed?” leaves them guessing.

Transparency continues after the action. People should be able to see what the agent did, which tool it used, and how to undo it if something went wrong. The more consequential the action, the more visible those steps should be.

Where visual interfaces still belong

Interfaces will still exist, just fewer. We expect the strongest products to combine conversation with visual UI exactly where visuals help.

Those moments are fairly consistent: reviewing results, comparing options, editing, approving and monitoring. A conversation is a fast way to ask for something. A table, a chart, or a side-by-side view often lets you judge what came back faster. Knowing when to switch between the two is a design decision in its own right.

Designers as system architects

As screens shrink, our attention shifts to how everything connects. We think less about individual pages and more about how users, agents, tools, data, and actions relate to each other. In that sense, designers are starting to work like system architects.

This work sits close to engineering. In our experience, it goes best when product designers and AI developers work through it together. The designer’s contribution is the human side of the system: what people expect, what they need to see, and where they need control.

Deciding when an interface is needed at all

The opportunity for designers is getting bigger. AI can generate UI quickly. As generation gets cheaper, deciding what should exist, what should disappear, and how the whole experience should behave becomes more valuable.

For years, product design has aimed for better interfaces. In the age of AI agents, part of the job is figuring out when an interface is needed at all, and designing everything around it when it isn’t.

entry.title: The Brand Color Strategy: Our Branding Agency’s Guide to Purposeful Design
entry.summary: Pantone picked white for 2026. Anjelika Lours’ Kour of DD.NYC explains why brand color strategy starts with what a color needs to do for the business.
entry.content:
Pantone picked white for 2026. Anjelika Lours’ Kour of DD.NYC explains why brand color strategy starts with what a color needs to do for the business.

About the Author:
DD.NYC® Creative Director & Managing Partner Anjelika Lours’ Kour specializes in corporate branding, web design, and video storytelling. Beyond working with powerhouse clients, she actively shapes the wider creative industry as a global judge for the International Academy of Digital Arts and Sciences (IADAS) and the Scholastic Art & Writing Awards.

There’s a spectrum of reasons for choosing brand colors. Maybe the client always loved blue, or it was the color of their first company logo. Maybe everyone else in the category is blue, so they want orange to stand out.

Instinct matters, but it isn’t a strategy on its own. After two decades of building brands across real estate, healthcare, hospitality, and technology, I care most about that distinction.

At our agency, brand color strategy sits alongside messaging and positioning. We ask clients what the color needs to do for their business. Personal preference comes up too, but only the business answer holds up once the brand launches.

That question gets more interesting once a year, when Pantone tells the world which color to pay attention to.

Why we don’t just chase the color of the year

Pantone has named a Color of the Year every December since 1999, and the ritual now reaches well past the design world. Retailers build seasonal collections around it. Interior and graphic designers reference it in client decks. It shows up everywhere before most consumers know why.

For 2026, Pantone did something new in the tradition’s history: it chose white. Cloud Dancer, officially PANTONE 11-4201, was introduced as a lofty, balanced white meant to symbolize calm in what Pantone called a frenetic society. It invites quiet reflection instead of more noise.

I understand the instinct behind it. Design has spent several years leaning into maximalism, saturated palettes, and loud everything, so a pause makes sense as a counter-movement. The reaction told a more useful story than the color itself. Critics called Cloud Dancer bland or tone-deaf, and several brands joked online that it looked like dairy. Even the most neutral color picks up meaning from the context it lands in.

Internally, we talk a lot about not chasing trends for their own sake. Our job is to work out which signals create lasting value for a brand and which ones are noise dressed up as insight.

Start with what the color needs to do

We don’t start a color conversation by opening a swatch book. We start by asking what the color needs to accomplish, and the answer changes with every brand. Three goals come up most often in our work: trust, exclusivity, and community.

When the goal is trust: WillowWood

Trust is usually the goal in finance, healthcare, and anything institutional. That means restraint, cooler tones, and choices that each earn their place. It was the thinking behind our corporate rebrand of WillowWood, a 117-year-old American prosthetics manufacturer that became WillowWood Global.

The palette had to do two jobs at once. It needed to feel clinical enough to earn a physician’s confidence and human enough to resonate with someone relearning how to walk. We kept the base to white, black, and light grey, and gave movement and vitality to a single turquoise accent.

Nothing in that palette was decorative. Every color carried part of the brand’s promise in a category where trust is the product. We introduced the new brand at Hanger Live with a custom trade show booth, and the rebrand later earned a Gold Anthem Award Honor in the Product and Innovation category.

When the goal is exclusivity: luxury real estate

For exclusivity, the instinct to add more color is almost always wrong. Our luxury real estate branding clients show this most clearly. Restraint, negative space, and a tightly limited palette read as confidence.

Add color for its own sake, and the brand starts to read as effort instead of ease. In luxury, effort is the opposite of what you’re selling.

When the goal is community: mission-led brands

For community or advocacy, warmth and saturation do more of the work than austerity ever could. Our approach to a mission-led, values-driven client looks nothing like our approach to a fintech startup, because the audience needs a different emotional register.

A palette that photographs beautifully but misses what the audience needs to feel hasn’t done its job yet.

Across all three, every color decision we make has to trace back to a specific outcome we can defend out loud. “It just felt right” doesn’t count. If we can’t explain what a color does for the business, we haven’t finished the work. We’ve just picked something that looks nice.

How to build a brand color palette with purpose

If you’re rethinking your brand’s palette, alone or with brand designers, this is roughly the process we’d walk a client through.

  1. Start by naming the job. Decide what the color needs to do: build trust, create urgency, signal premium positioning, or feel warm and approachable. Write it down in one sentence before a single hex code enters the conversation.
  2. Audit your category honestly. Look at what competitors do with color and ask a harder question than “do I like it?” Is it working for them, or is it a default nobody has questioned in years?
  3. Test restraint before you test more. Adding color is the easy move. Subtracting it and trusting the remaining choices to carry more weight is usually the harder, more confident one.
  4. Make the reasoning visible. Whatever palette you land on, write the “why” into your brand guidelines and pitch materials. If the reasoning needs a long defense, the palette probably needs more work.

Stop treating color as decoration

Every decision we make at DD.NYC comes back to one question: what is this doing for the business? Color doesn’t get an exception because it’s visual, emotional, and easy to have opinions about. Treating it as decoration is one of the most common mistakes we see founders make, and one of the easiest to fix.

Before you pick your next brand color, or reach for whatever Pantone declares next December, ask one question. Could you defend this choice, out loud, in one sentence? If the answer is no, you don’t have a color decision yet.

entry.title: How to Build a Brand That Doesn’t Look Like Everyone Else
entry.summary: Competitor research tells you where you fit, and copying it makes you forgettable. Diana Hlevnjak on how to build a brand that stands apart in its category.
entry.content:
Competitor research tells you where you fit, and copying it makes you forgettable. Diana Hlevnjak on how to build a brand that stands apart in its category.

About the Author:
Diana Hlevnjak brings over 20 years of experience in graphic design, branding, and illustration. Her Master’s degree in Fine Arts continues to inform her approach to visual communication, blending artistic exploration with practical design thinking. Her work spans branding, packaging, game design, and illustration, always centered on building cohesive, thoughtful visual systems across digital and print media.

When you start a new brand, it is natural to look at what already exists. You look at competitors, collect references, save logos you like, and build a moodboard. You might even look for a brand designer who has already worked in your industry. Learning how to build a brand often starts with that research, and it shouldn’t end there.

It makes sense. You want someone who understands your market.

The problem is that if you look too closely at what everyone in your category does, your brand can end up looking like everyone else. A strong brand needs to understand its category. It doesn’t always need to look like it.

Learn your category’s visual language before you move away from it

Every industry develops its own visual language. Coffee brands lean toward certain aesthetics. Technology companies have their own conventions. Beauty, wellness, hospitality, finance, food, and fashion all have patterns that become familiar over time.

These conventions are useful. They help people understand at a glance what kind of product or service they’re looking at.

Understanding that visual language and repeating it are two different things. If every competitor uses the same typography, color palette, symbols, and visual style, following them too closely can make your brand feel both appropriate and forgettable.

The aim is to find your difference, which rarely means being completely different. Start by understanding what your category expects. Then decide where your brand follows those expectations and where it moves away.

Start with the problem before the logo

Before you brief logo designers, a few questions need answers:

  • Who are you trying to reach?
  • What makes your business different?
  • What should people feel when they encounter your brand?
  • What does your category already look like?
  • Where are the opportunities to do something differently?
  • What needs to stay familiar, and what can be unexpected?

These questions create the foundation for every design decision. Without them, it is easy to reproduce whatever is popular right now.

Stepping away from coffee category clichés with ALTITUDE

ALTITUDE is a specialty coffee brand identity I created for enthusiasts who appreciate quality, craftsmanship, and origin. The collection covers three single-origin coffees from Ethiopia, Colombia, and Guatemala. My work covered the logo and packaging design.

Coffee is a category full of familiar imagery: beans, cups and vintage badges. The challenge was to communicate premium quality through subtle design choices, while keeping three distinct products connected in one visual system.

I built the identity around altitude, a defining characteristic of premium coffee cultivation. Instead of literal illustrations, I used abstract, flowing forms inspired by mountain contours as the core visual language. A custom wordmark, a restrained color palette, and minimalist typography create a calm, contemporary aesthetic.

Each pouch has its own color composition, roast profile, and origin information. The goal was a line that feels cohesive while each origin keeps its own personality, without the beans, cups and badges the category usually relies on.

Look for inspiration outside your industry

This is one reason I don’t believe a designer’s portfolio should be judged only by whether they have worked in your industry.

I often notice that clients looking for a designer ask to see work similar to what they need. A restaurant wants to see restaurant branding. A skincare company wants skincare branding. A technology company wants technology branding.

There is logic behind this request. You want reassurance that the designer understands your world. There is another way to look at it, though. Sometimes the most interesting solution for your brand comes from somewhere completely different. A designer who has worked across many industries has faced different problems, audiences, visual languages, and ways to communicate an idea.

Borrow principles from other categories

Imagine you’re launching a premium tea brand. You don’t need a designer who has already created five tea brands.

You might find inspiration in how a luxury fashion brand uses typography, how an architecture studio builds a visual system, how a fragrance brand uses negative space, or how a publishing house organizes information. None of those businesses sell tea, and that is exactly why the references can be useful.

Judge a designer’s portfolio by how they think

When evaluating a designer, look at their work as a whole. Don’t only ask whether they have designed something exactly like your business. Also ask what kinds of problems they have solved.

Look at the variety, and at how they approached different audiences. Check whether they can move between visual languages, and how they use typography, color, illustration, symbols, patterns, and composition. Above all, look for the thinking behind the work.

A designer who has created identities across very different industries brings something valuable: the ability to see your category from the outside. That perspective makes it easier to spot opportunities that someone immersed in the category might overlook. In my own branding and illustration work, projects range from beverage and food brands to law practices and SaaS platforms.

Use competitor research to find your place

Competitive research matters. A designer should understand the landscape your brand will enter. That research should help answer “Where do we fit?” It shouldn’t automatically answer “What should we look like?”

If ten competitors use muted neutrals, you don’t have to use a bright color. If everyone has a minimalist wordmark, you don’t automatically need an expressive logo. If everyone uses an illustrated mascot, you don’t need another one just because it is common.

Sometimes differentiation is obvious, and sometimes it is subtle. It might be a typographic detail, an unexpected proportion, a distinctive visual system, an illustration language, a particular use of color, or a different way of organizing information. Quiet differences can be just as recognizable as loud ones.

Give your designer room to surprise you

If you’re hiring a designer, it is tempting to arrive with a specific picture of what you want. You may already have a favorite font, a color palette, a symbol, a few competitor brands you admire, and a Pinterest board full of references.

Those things are helpful. They communicate your taste and show a designer what resonates with you. Treat them as a starting point, and leave room for the destination to change.

Sometimes the most valuable thing a designer brings is a connection you wouldn’t have made yourself. It might come from another industry, a visual principle you hadn’t considered, or a solution that looks nothing like your references but still feels more like your brand.

That is part of the value of hiring a designer. Good design goes beyond executing the picture already in your head. It helps you discover a visual identity you might not have reached on your own, one that makes your brand recognizable, relevant, and distinctly yours.

entry.title: The Death of Default SaaS: Why AI Makes Product Design More Important
entry.summary: Quincy Samycia replaced five SaaS subscriptions with one AI-built platform. Here is why the experience put product design at the center of build-versus-buy decisions.
entry.content:
Quincy Samycia replaced five SaaS subscriptions with one AI-built platform. Here is why the experience put product design at the center of build-versus-buy decisions.

About the Author:
Quincy Samycia is Head of Brand and Growth at The Branded Agency, a branding, creative, website, and growth agency working with ambitious companies across Canada, the United States, and international markets. He helps organizations connect brand strategy with the creative, digital experiences and marketing systems responsible for measurable growth.

Over the past two months, I replaced Asana, Toggl, HubSpot, Typeform, and Calendly at The Branded Agency with custom software I built using AI. The experience changed how I think about product design.

The work took less than 250 hours in total. We kept the design quality and functionality the agency needed, and gained capabilities our previous subscriptions did not include, such as enterprise-tier functions. I now estimate annual subscription savings above US$20,000.

That figure is an annualized subscription estimate. A full return-on-investment calculation would still need to account for my time, AI services, hosting, and maintenance.

The bigger change was bringing functions from five tools into one platform designed around our agency. Instead of adapting to someone else’s product, I could decide how our software should work.

I do not think every software-as-a-service company is about to disappear. I do think SaaS is losing its place as the unquestioned default. For designers, that opens a wider brief: shaping the systems businesses run on, along with the screens people see.

Five subscriptions replaced by one custom platform

I did not build five separate clones. I combined what we needed from project management, time tracking, customer relationship management, forms, and scheduling into one platform designed around how our agency operates.

Vendors sell those functions as separate products, but the work is connected. Clients have projects. Projects have tasks. Tasks consume time. That time affects capacity, client balances, and reporting. Building our own software let me design those relationships together instead of organizing our work around tool boundaries.

I set out to replace what we depended on, add what our subscriptions lacked, and give our team a consistent experience. We never aimed to reproduce every vendor feature.

That is the shift in the build-versus-buy decision. Replacing established software no longer has to mean buying another vendor’s version. It can mean building a system that fits the business better.

The product is in the connections

Time tracking makes this tangible. I designed our workflow so logged hours come off the client balance, while new entries stay editable until the team member submits the day for review. Reporting can then filter to approved time for invoicing.

The timer stays available across the workspace, with controls for projects, tasks, and tags. Reports combine date ranges, clients, projects, people and tags, with options for grouping, rounding, CSV export and client sharing.

What matters is how these pieces connect. Recording work, reviewing it, and communicating it are part of the same process.

Those are product decisions. When should time affect a balance? What can someone edit before submitting it? Which entries belong in a client report? AI can help implement the answers, but the answers have to come from understanding the business.

AI assistance needs a visible boundary

AI helped me build the software, and I also designed AI assistance into it.

The planner suggests task priorities, flags slipping work, and proposes due dates. Its instruction to the user is explicit: nothing changes until you accept it.

The project-finish view is organized around remaining work, assignments, working hours, meetings, and time off. A useful plan needs that context. It must reflect what the team can deliver and which tasks are urgent.

The assistant focuses on operational tasks. It finds missing hours, due dates, or assignees, updates client goal hours, and prepares bulk reassignments or deadline changes. A separate staged-changes panel gives those suggestions a visible place to be reviewed.

That boundary matters. Suggesting a deadline and committing a team to it are different actions. A good interface makes the distinction clear instead of hiding it behind an impressive chat response.

This is where product design matters most as implementation speeds up. Navigation, hierarchy, editable states, and review steps decide whether new capabilities are useful. Design determines what a business’s software should make possible, and that work starts before the AI writes any code.

The build-versus-buy shift is already happening

Tools such as ChatGPT and Codex, Claude, and Lovable offer different routes into AI-assisted software development. None of them removes the need for requirements or technical judgment.

Retool’s 2026 Build vs. Buy report surveyed 817 customers and builders in late 2025. It found that 35% of teams had replaced at least one SaaS tool with a custom build. Because this is vendor-sponsored research among builders, it reflects early adopters more than the broader business landscape.

In August 2026, Reuters reported that Lovable said users had created more than 60 million projects since its launch. That number measures experimentation and says little about successful production deployments. The scale still helps explain why building now comes up in conversations once dominated by buying.

My experience is one example, and other businesses may not see the same savings. It is still a reason to rethink who can build and what custom software costs.

Moving faster still comes with responsibility

A small agency can test a bounded workflow with a few people. A large company may have legacy integrations, procurement requirements, training needs, and competing departmental priorities. Switching costs can outweigh subscription savings, even when building gets cheaper.

Some hesitation comes from unfamiliarity. Some reflects real operational risk. I expect smaller businesses with clear workflows to move first, while larger organizations may build around existing systems before replacing them.

Enterprise-tier features do not equal enterprise readiness. A useful interface says nothing about security, reliability, or compliance.

In May 2026, WIRED reported that researchers had found more than 5,000 AI-built web apps with little or no access protection. Vendors disputed parts of the findings and pointed to configuration choices. The lesson I take is to treat deployment with the same care as the build.

Lovable’s own guidance says automated checks do not replace a thorough security review. Before relying on a custom system, I would require tested permissions, protected credentials, restorable backups, monitoring, documentation, and a named maintenance owner. Sensitive or critical workflows need review from experienced AI developers and security specialists.

The economics must include ongoing operation and support. Replacing five subscriptions still leaves us dependent on infrastructure providers. Two months of building also cannot show what years of maintenance will cost.

The opportunity is to design how a business works

I see a larger opportunity than another fixed application: systems that help companies build, customize, and govern tools around their own needs. The companies providing those systems will still be software companies. What changes is what customers buy.

For product designers and agencies, the opportunity is to translate business knowledge into usable products. Understand the workflow, define the relationships, make decisions visible, and leave something others can maintain. Generating screens is only one part of that work.

Start with one process worth improving. Define success, prototype with non-sensitive data, test with actual users, and plan a controlled transition. Keep the tools that still earn their place.

I expect SaaS to stay. I also expect every subscription to justify why buying it beats building the part we need.

The saving gets attention. The ability to design how our business works is what makes the change matter.

 ⁠

entry.title: Website Design That Converts: Why Good-Looking Sites Still Fail
entry.summary: Beautiful photos stop the scroll, but they rarely explain the service. Klym Yevtushenko of VibeStyle on website design that converts premium visitors into inquiries.
entry.content:
Beautiful photos stop the scroll, but they rarely explain the service. Klym Yevtushenko of VibeStyle on website design that converts premium visitors into inquiries.

About the Author:
Klym Yevtushenko is the Founder & CEO of VibeStyle. He works with startups and growing companies to turn ideas into clear, engaging digital experiences: from high-converting websites, landing pages, and mobile apps to SaaS platforms and digital products.

A beautifully lit room can stop a scroll. It cannot, by itself, explain how to get one. That gap is where many premium service websites lose people, and closing it is the core of website design that converts.

Eclectic Lighting is a Dutch lighting consultancy founded in 2020 by Rick Hommel. The studio combines lighting advice, design, product supply and installation, with work across homes, offices, public buildings, shops and showrooms. Its homepage states the philosophy early: light is part of the architecture, from concept to realization.

Our job was to build a premium, image-led website that does more than look good. It had to help homeowners, architects, and business owners understand the service, see relevant expertise, trust the process, and start an inquiry. The first half comes naturally to most web designers. The second half decides whether the site earns its keep.

Why good-looking websites lose visitors before the inquiry

Lighting is unusually visual. A photograph can make a room look exceptional, but it cannot tell a potential client what the collaboration involves. It also cannot show where the process starts or whether the studio works on their kind of property. Visitors admire a project and still leave without getting in touch.

I think of this as the gap between inspiration and action. A premium site needs bridges that close the gap. On Eclectic Lighting, there are four: project filters by sector, a clear four-step process, specific client reviews, and a floor plan upload. Each one answers a question the photography leaves open.

Photography that leads somewhere

Project photography is essential for a lighting studio. It is the closest a visitor gets to standing in the finished room. Every strong image should still lead somewhere.

On the site, each featured project opens into its own page, like the Deza Kozijnen showroom, with a “view project” link placed on the image. A visitor who stops to admire a room has an obvious next click. We kept the imagery immersive and gave it a direction. The same principle runs through the premium websites in our portfolio, from real estate to chauffeur services.

Four steps that make a bespoke service feel approachable

Premium services often feel abstract from the outside. Prospective clients cannot picture what happens after the first call, so some never make it.

Eclectic Lighting’s process has four steps. It starts with an introduction meeting at the office or on site. The design step produces a 2D lighting plan that shows which light goes where. In the presentation, the client sees that plan alongside a fixture book. Realization follows with a no-obligation quote, and the team can coordinate with the architect, interior designer, installer, and contractor.

Laid out in sequence on the homepage, those steps turn a bespoke service into something a visitor can picture. That reduces uncertainty without making the service feel transactional.

A portfolio organized by the visitor’s context

A homeowner renovating a kitchen and an architect specifying lighting for a public building look for different evidence. One wants to see a home like theirs. The other wants proof that the studio can handle scale and coordination.

The portfolio filters projects into commercial, residential, public buildings, and shops and showrooms. That turns a gallery into a set of answers. Visitors can find work that matches their own project and judge relevance before they judge beauty.

Reviews that make expertise believable

Generic quality claims do little on a premium site. Specific client experiences do more. Eclectic Lighting shows a 4.9 out of 5 rating from 28 reviews, along with longer testimonials.

The longer ones carry the weight. Homeowners describe detailed lighting plans and fixtures labeled to match the plan, which made their installer’s job easier. Interior architects describe repeat collaborations and reliable delivery. Those details tell a new visitor what it feels like to work with the studio, in a way no adjective can.

The floor plan upload as a natural next step

Most contact forms ask visitors to “get started” without telling them what that means. Eclectic Lighting asks for something visitors already have. The contact section invites them to upload a floor plan and receive a no-obligation cost indication for their lighting plan.

That request matches the service. People arrive with a renovation, a deadline, and often a drawing from their architect. Asking for the floor plan lets them bring their actual project into the conversation. It also asks more of web development than a standard form, because the upload has to accept PDFs, Word files, and images.

For visitors who prefer a quick question, a WhatsApp help link sits on the page. Small entry points like these are worth checking on every screen size, and good UI/UX designers treat them as part of the conversion path.

The test I use before a premium website goes live

After a visitor admires the work, do they know whether the studio fits their project, and how to begin? If the answer is yes, the site is doing both of its jobs. If not, the photography is carrying more than it should.

Premium design should feel effortless for the visitor, all the way from the first image to the first inquiry. That is the standard we apply to every website and landing page design we take on.

entry.title: Strategic Thinking for Designers: What “Be More Strategic” Actually Means
entry.summary: Leadership keeps asking designers to be more strategic. Vicente Reyes Montealegre of Afternow breaks down strategic thinking for designers into three habits and three questions.
entry.content:
Leadership keeps asking designers to be more strategic. Vicente Reyes Montealegre of Afternow breaks down strategic thinking for designers into three habits and three questions.

About the Author:
Vicente Reyes Montealegre heads Afternow’s Brand and Web teams, guiding SaaS companies, enterprises, and fast-growing startups through their digital journeys. The agency’s work spans strategy, brand, website, product and development, all under one roof and connected to one vision.

If you are an in-house designer or work at an agency, you have probably heard it from leadership: “We need to be more strategic.” They usually say it with conviction and rarely explain it. That makes it feel important and hard to act on, especially when nobody shows you what it looks like.

You might read it as a request to become a brand strategist or a product strategist. Much of what follows overlaps with those roles, but this piece is about strategic thinking for designers at any level.

Strategic thinking sits close to the root of design itself. To design is to plan, to project, to give something intention and purpose. That intention only holds up when it is grounded in the context the work has to live in. In my experience, building a strategic mindset into your daily work is one of the clearest signs you are ready for your next career move.

What it looks like when strategic thinking is missing

When the comment comes, it usually points to one of three things.

  • Not knowing how the business works. Whether it’s your employer or a client, the gaps show up in comments and meetings. A designer may not know how the company makes money, who buys and uses the product, or what it needs to stay ahead.
  • Working in a silo. The design role becomes a list of tasks, disconnected from the people around it. A brand designer lays out the sales deck without asking what the sales team needs it to do. A product designer polishes a flow without knowing what the feature is meant to move. At team level, designers end up working for designers, producing good work that rarely connects to the rest of the operation.
  • Talking about design only in design terms. The work might be strong, but the case for it is made in craft language. Leadership hears grids, type, and consistency, but listens for growth, efficiency, and risk. The value gets lost in translation.

What strategic thinking looks like in practice

Leaving jargon aside, being strategic is a way of thinking. It shows in the questions you ask, how you weigh trade-offs and how you get from evidence to a conclusion. It also shows in how you define success beyond the immediate ask, and how you decide when things are uncertain.

Much of it is visible in how you show up in a room. Arrive with uncertainty, complaints, or opinions, and you hand the problem to someone else. Arrive with curiosity, clarity, or a recommendation, and you take ownership. When you explain how you landed there, including your assumptions and trade-offs, you give the room your reasoning. Even if your call turns out to be wrong, people have something concrete to build on.

That holds at any level, from team lead to a first senior role. Here are three habits and three questions that help.

1. Know where the business is going

Whatever company or client you work with, a basic understanding of the business and its industry should inform your approach. What value does the company bring? How does it make money? Which customers does it want next?

Most designers get a version of this in a discovery session, a roadmap, or a leadership update. Many skim past it as someone else’s job. It is yours too. Design is one of the main ways a company’s direction becomes visible, on its website, in a pitch deck, across marketing channels, and in the product itself.

Once you know where the business is heading, you can ask the strategic question: how is my work helping us get there?

2. Look beyond your design team

You probably work alongside project managers, developers, marketers, sales, and HR, and sooner or later their requests land on your desk.

Learning how those teams operate, and how your work supports theirs, changes how they see you. Design can improve how a company works internally. Think of smoother design system handovers to development, more usable marketing assets, or internal initiatives that build culture. Each of these small wins shows other teams the value of design first-hand.

Once you understand how other teams work, you can ask the strategic question: how can we improve how we work together?

3. Connect your work to what leadership values

Presenting work gets harder when the audience is unfamiliar with design or sits in senior leadership.

The same principle applies here: design for your audience. With a client or senior leader, start by understanding what they value. Lead with the bottom line, keep it high-level, and bring solutions. Show what your design affects and how it supports company goals, so people can decide quickly.

Working on a better-looking website? Explain how a better structure can bring in more leads. Building a new design system? Explain how much time it saves as the product scales.

Once you know what your audience values, you can ask the strategic question: why should my work matter to them?

How we built strategic thinking into Afternow

Leadership asked our whole company to be more strategic, too.

We have made most of the mistakes in this article. We gave our team too little visibility of the business and financial decisions behind the agency, which left people disconnected from the market. We worked in silos, handing tasks between teams without guardrails or a shared sense of direction. And we bored more than one client with design jargon, focusing on how things looked over the value we brought.

We are in a very different place than five years ago, with plenty of room left to improve. Today we treat strategy as a service and as a mindset across every team, from design and development to sales and HR. These are some of the initiatives our designers have worked on over the past year.

  • Defining our own brand. As part of becoming Afternow, we brought our team leads together to pin down who we are. We defined the value we bring, what makes us different, the services we provide, what we can prove, and where we want to be in a few years.
  • Sharing how we use AI. Designers used to explore AI alone. Now we evaluate tools together and decide what belongs in our processes.
  • Smoother handovers. From UX wireframes to branding, web and product design, and on to development, we build design systems, modules, and templates that move between teams with less friction. Less time on translation, more on execution.
  • Everyone at the table from day one. On client projects, strategists, designers, and developers join from the start. We weigh every decision or pivot against the work that follows.
  • Rethinking how we present. We keep adjusting our presentations to what matters to the client. What we once called “playful” or “creative,” we now frame as “impactful.” “Serious and understated” has become “scalable” or “manageable,” language that matches what marketing managers care about.

None of these initiatives rely on one person. Each connects to what the business needs: our value, our workflows, and our alignment with clients.

Where craft fits into strategic design

Many of us came to design for the details: the craft, the concept, how a single typographic choice or color can carry a story. Some well-established designers have stayed far from corporate dynamics and built remarkable careers, with work that reaches people in ways no spreadsheet could back up.

Nothing here asks you to give that up. The care behind a typeface or a micro-interaction is already a series of decisions about intention and purpose, which is what strategic thinking is. Grounding that intention in the business, the teams around you, and your impact gives the care direction. It also earns the craft the time and trust it needs. Often, the most persuasive strategic argument in the room is the work itself, made well.

Widening the brief

In the early 2000s, design thinking carried the designer’s process into boardrooms and business schools. UX and product design brought designers closer to how companies build and grow. Today, more product designers are founding companies, and generative AI is raising real questions about our role.

Strategic thinking has been the constant through every shift. Each time, designers had to adapt to new actors, trends and industries, and decide what design should take responsibility for next. As someone in daily contact with culture, businesses and people, you are well placed to do the same.

If you are still unsure what “be more strategic” means where you work, ask. If the answer is clear, you have your brief. If it isn’t, helping define it might be the most strategic place to start.

 ⁠

entry.title: Community Growth for Food and Beverage Brands: From First Shelf to Lasting Fans
entry.summary: Followers watch, communities buy. Aaron Swinton, Founder of MAVRK Studio, explains how community growth for food and beverage brands starts before the first day on the shelf.
entry.content:
Followers watch, communities buy. Aaron Swinton, Founder of MAVRK Studio, explains how community growth for food and beverage brands starts before the first day on the shelf.

About the Author:
Aaron Swinton is the Founder and CEO of MAVRK Studio, where he handles business strategy, client partnerships, and the agency’s growth. He has experience in brand building, venture investing, fundraising, and operations, and he uses it to help CPG brands launch and grow.

Most food and beverage founders I meet can tell me their follower count. Fewer can tell me how many people have tasted the product, bought it twice, or asked a local store to stock it. That second set of numbers is what I mean by community. It is also where community growth for food and beverage brands starts.

For a CPG brand launching in 2026, community growth is the system that connects real people to a new product before, during, and after it reaches shelves. It shapes your first 90 days on the Whole Foods shelf and what happens after the first thousands of people taste the product. Over time, it shows up in sell-through, reorders, and how investors value the brand.

This piece is for funded founders and brand managers preparing a launch or relaunch. At MAVRK Studio, community growth is part of our integrated 90-day launch system, and the lessons here come from that work.

What community growth means for a food and beverage brand

Followers watch. A community buys, buys again, and tells other people. The difference matters most in categories where the first purchase is a bet on taste.

Think of a kombucha brand, an RTD coffee, or a frozen meal line. Each one depends on someone trying it, liking it, and finding it again on a crowded shelf. Community growth builds the paths between those moments, from a launch-event guest to a repeat shopper who follows the brand on social media.

Our order of work stays the same: validate the category, define the position, then build community around that position. A community designed before day one on shelf has something specific to gather around. One added after launch often has to figure out what the brand stands for publicly.

Why community work starts before the product hits the shelf

Our 90-day system runs in four phases: foundation, build, pre-launch, and launch. Community planning starts as soon as you define the product and vision, often before the packaging is final. Starting early helps founders avoid costly mistakes in positioning, packaging, and go-to-market strategy.

Roughly, the first month covers foundation, the second covers build, and the final weeks cover pre-launch and launch. Community work runs in parallel with production and packaging. The timeline extends only when a product is complex or production slips.

Many founders run a launch through separate agencies for social, events, PR, and retail. Each can do good work, and the brand still feels different in every channel. We keep strategy, creative, photography, and content under one team in our Brooklyn studio, so people see one brand from the first post to the first tasting.

How Folkland’s farm story built an audience before launch

Foundation is the phase that gives community work something to hold on to. Before we plan a single post, we work with founders on the messaging hierarchy, origin story, founder story, visual toolkit, and brand voice. Our strategists and packaging designers share that groundwork, so the shelf and the feed say the same thing.

Folkland came to us from a multi-generational family manufacturing business. They had developed a health-conscious French fry but had no defined marketing strategy, and retail expansion was coming. The brand needed to explain why it was different and earn credibility before it reached stores.

We built a story-led social strategy around the farm, the people behind the product, and the journey from potato to shelf. Our work covered social and content strategy, photography and video, community management and the launch campaign. The pre-launch campaign built an initial social audience, and the launch supported Folkland’s rollout across more than 1,100 retail locations.

Clarity on who a product is for and what role it plays in their life guides everything that follows. For Folkland, the farm and the family behind it gave every piece of content a reason to exist.

Building a digital home on the right social media platforms

Even a retail-first CPG brand needs a digital home before launch. Shoppers who spot the product in store look it up, and they should find the same brand they saw on the shelf.

For most food and beverage brands in 2026, we prioritize Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube Shorts. LinkedIn sometimes joins the mix when the brand needs a B2B story for retail buyers and investors. Our brand designers set up a consistent identity across social profiles, a landing page, and a simple ecommerce or pre-order flow.

Owned channels carry as much weight as social. A pre-launch waitlist or a founding members email and SMS list gives the brand people it can reach without an algorithm. A refrigerated beverage might build that list through local pre-order pickups. A shelf-stable snack can open national pre-orders and ship directly.

IRL experiences that turn a tasting into a relationship

People taste food before they trust it, so in-person experiences sit at the center of our community work. A single launch event creates a moment. A planned series of touchpoints creates the repeat visits and repeat purchases a brand needs.

That series can include in-store demos and tastings, founder-hosted pop-ups, collab dinners with local restaurants, and stalls at food festivals or farmers’ markets.

For Reali, a protein ice cream we launched from identity to retail shelf, we brought the product to athletic audiences in person. The brand had to communicate indulgence, protein, and real ingredients without feeling like diet food. Putting a cup in the hands of active people let them taste that proposition directly. Reali entered more than 15 retail locations within two months of launch.

Every in-person moment should feed the digital community. We plan QR codes at demos, SMS opt-ins at events, photo moments, and a branded hashtag before the first sample goes out. A well-captured one-day launch event can provide recap content, fan reposts, and email follow-ups for weeks afterward.

Pointing community at the retail shelf

Getting into retail is hard in 2026, and staying on shelf is harder without people asking for the product. We coordinate community work with retail readiness, including co-packer, distributor, and broker readiness.

Each retailer can become a small community hub. Localized promotions, store staff education, in-aisle signage, and co-branded social posts all point people to a specific shelf. A “Try us at H-E-B in Austin this month” campaign gives followers a clear next step.

A brand that arrives at a buyer meeting with an engaged audience has a stronger case for getting listed and reordered. That audience also gives the product its first shoppers once it is listed.

The first 90 days after launch and the metrics we watch

Launch day is when community work starts in earnest. Launch week brings the event and the first wave of content. Weeks two to four set up a weekly social series and recurring in-store demos. Weeks five to eight add monthly collab events and founder AMAs, and weeks nine to twelve move toward seasonal campaigns.

We review performance throughout that window and adjust content, events, and retail focus as results come in. Engagement, saves, shares, and user-generated content show what resonates on social media platforms. We tie those signals back to samplings, sign-ups and repeat purchases.

On the IRL side, we watch the demo-to-follow ratio, event sign-ups, email and SMS list growth, and sample-to-purchase lift. Sell-through during promotion windows and retailer velocity show whether the community is reaching the shelf. Follower counts come last on that list.

After 90 days, some brands keep growing with us. Others take the system and playbook we built and run it in-house. Either way, the goal is a food and beverage brand with real people around it who keep coming back.
