entry.title: Small Business Website Design After AI: Nobody Commissions the Plumber's Website Anymore
entry.summary: AI website builders took the bottom rung of small business website design. Boris Sage of DesWave explains what clients still pay a design studio for.
entry.content:
AI website builders took the bottom rung of small business website design. Boris Sage of DesWave explains what clients still pay a design studio for.

About the Author:
Boris Sage is the Principal Consultant at DesWave, a design and development agency helping businesses build websites, e-commerce platforms, and brand identities that convert visitors into customers.

We run a design and branding studio. Most of what I do sits between the people who need design and the people who make it, so I see a lot of inbound. Over the last year, something shifted in that inbound. I have not seen it described properly anywhere, so I am going to describe it.

Every inquiry now arrives with an artifact attached.

A logo generated from a prompt. A landing page someone put together in an afternoon. Increasingly, a whole site, already live, with the domain already pointed at it. Two years ago, people wrote to me describing what they wanted. Now they send me a file and ask what I think.

That shift is changing small business website design faster than most studios admit, and it has changed how I talk about our work.

Why I stopped saying AI only makes design work faster

For most of this year, I said AI makes the work faster without taking anybody’s job. I said it on calls. I put it in emails. I believed it, because it was true of my own studio.

I have stopped saying it, and the reason is worth explaining.

Somebody used to build the plumber’s website. The barber’s, the roofer’s, the mobile dog groomer’s. Four or five pages, a contact form, a gallery, and a phone number. It was unglamorous work, but it was a real book of business. For many independent web designers, it was the whole book.

That work has left.

The plumber now builds the site himself in the evening with an AI website builder. It is fine, and fine is what he needed. The demand is still there, but it moved into tools that cost less than any designer. People who couldn’t move up the market with it are gone.

So the accurate version is that the market floor was deleted. The people still standing are the ones who could climb. I happen to be one of them, which is exactly why I believed the comfortable version for so long.

“Can you just clean this up?” Three checks for AI-built websites

Here is what replaced the floor, in my inbox at least.

People arrive having built something, and they ask for refinement. Polish. A few professional touches. Sometimes that is precisely right, and a few hundred dollars of work gets them where they want to be.

Often, it is a rebuild wearing refinement’s clothes.

The difference is almost never visible from the front of the site. It sits in three places:

  1. Whether anybody non-technical can change a paragraph of text without calling somebody.
  2. Whether the site can be exported, or whether it is welded into the tool it was made in.
  3. Whether the logo exists as a vector or only as a PNG. Logo designers work in vector because it decides whether the mark can ever go on a sign, a van or anything embroidered.

A site that fails all three is a good-looking prototype, however finished it appears. A prototype is a genuinely different object from a product. Prototypes are supposed to look finished. That is their entire point.

This is now the hardest commercial conversation of my week, and I don’t think our industry has worked out how to have it yet. The client believes they are buying the last mile. You are looking at the first one. Quote the last mile, and you lose money. Quote the first, and you sound like you are inventing problems to inflate an invoice.

I now walk people through those three checks before I quote anything, so they reach the conclusion rather than me. It has not failed me yet. I wrote a longer version for business owners, covering the checks and what they actually mean. The more owners self-diagnose before they call anyone, the better the conversation goes for everybody.

What I got wrong about clients arriving with AI drafts

I assumed a client arriving with a draft would make my job easier. It would be a starting point, a reference, something to react to instead of a blank page.

It makes production easier. It makes consulting considerably harder, and I didn’t notice that for months.

When a client arrived with an idea in their head, it was soft. You put three or four directions in front of them, and the imagined version quietly dissolves. It was never really a picture. It was a feeling wearing the costume of a picture. They pick the direction that actually works, and they are usually relieved.

A rendered draft does not dissolve. They have already seen their idea executed, and they are attached to one specific version, with a particular typeface and a particular blue. The question has quietly shifted from “what should this be” to “can you make this better.” Those two questions do not produce the same answer.

The cost shows up in the most expensive place. The generated draft is competent and generic, because the model averages everything it has ever seen. Generic is the one thing a small business cannot afford when it needs to look different from four competitors in the same town. You are now arguing against an artifact instead of a vague preference, and artifacts win arguments.

I do not have a clean solution. What has helped is asking one question early, before anyone falls in love with anything: what will this brand have to do in a room you are not in? It asks about the job before the look. That question has no draft attached, so it reopens the space the draft closed.

What AI did not change about design project timelines

Production time has come down. I will not pretend otherwise, and studios claiming nothing has changed aren’t being straight with anyone.

Production time was never what made projects long, though.

The gap between a four-week project and a ten-week project almost never comes from how fast anyone draws. It comes from how long feedback takes to arrive, how scattered it is when it does, and how many people must agree before anything moves. A logo project can be sold honestly as two weeks and still run five. Not a single hour of that delay happens at a desk.

No model has touched that, and I do not think one will. It is a decision problem, and decisions live in the client’s calendar.

Which is mildly funny, when you think about it. We got faster at the part that was never the bottleneck.

When clients assume your design studio uses AI

This comes up constantly, and designers get defensive. I think the defensiveness is a mistake.

Clients increasingly assume we use AI somewhere in the process. We do, in places, and I am not interested in pretending otherwise. Being seen as a studio that has adapted is better than being seen as one that has not.

It only works as an asset when it comes with a clear answer about what clients pay for that the tool does not do. On its own, “they assume you use AI” becomes a discount argument the client builds in their own head. It is the same pressure that deleted the floor of the market.

My answer, for what it is worth, has four parts. Clients pay for judgment about what to build before they spend money building it. They pay for the parts that have to survive print, embroidery, signage, and a phone screen in sunlight. They pay for a system, not a file. And they pay for somebody who is accountable in eight months when something breaks.

That is a shorter list than it was three years ago. I also think it is a more honest one.

Where I have landed on AI and small business design

The optimistic and pessimistic reads are both partly right, which is why the argument never resolves.

AI came for the bottom rung of the ladder, which happened to be the rung most people used to climb on. The work above it got more interesting and, in my experience, better paid. The work below it is gone and won’t come back.

If you are early in your career and planned to learn the trade by building small business sites, that route is closing. Learn the judgment part instead: working out what a business actually needs before anyone opens a design tool. That is the piece that survived. Most people who arrive in my inbox with a finished-looking draft have no idea they skipped it.

I do not know how much of this will still be true in a year. Ask me then.

 ⁠

entry.title: The Cost of Endless Options: Why AI Branding Needs Creative Direction
entry.summary: AI can generate a hundred brand directions in an afternoon. Quincy Samycia of The Branded Agency explains why AI branding needs creative direction to turn that abundance into a recognizable brand.
entry.content:
AI can generate a hundred brand directions in an afternoon. Quincy Samycia of The Branded Agency explains why AI branding needs creative direction to turn that abundance into a recognizable brand.

About the Author:
Quincy Samycia is Head of Brand and Growth at The Branded Agency, a branding, creative, website, and growth agency working with ambitious companies across Canada, the United States, and international markets. He helps organizations connect brand strategy with the creative, digital experiences and marketing systems responsible for measurable growth.

Generative AI can now produce in an afternoon what once took a creative team several days. Names, headlines, moodboards, and campaign concepts arrive almost on request. That is real progress, and it changes the problem creative leaders have to solve. The bottleneck is moving from the cost of making an option to the judgment needed to choose one.

At The Branded Agency, we use AI to accelerate research, exploration, and production. I do not think defending slow work is a serious strategy. A 2023 experiment published in Science found that ChatGPT cut time spent on professional writing tasks by 40% and raised evaluated output quality by 18%.

Speed still leaves the direction open. A business can generate a hundred plausible identities before it answers the question that should govern them all: what are we trying to make recognizable?

The tools create abundance. Brands are built through selection, coherence, and repetition, and AI does none of those on its own. That gap is why AI branding needs creative direction.

Abundance changes the creative problem

The 2026 AI Index from Stanford HAI reports that 70% of surveyed organizations use generative AI in at least one business function. AI-assisted production is now part of the normal environment in which brands compete. Early adopters no longer own it as an advantage.

When every competitor can produce more campaign routes, landing pages, and social assets, output stops being scarce. More competent-looking material does not automatically create more meaning.

Generative systems quickly produce a polished interpretation of a category. Ask for a modern technology brand, and you get something that looks familiar. That helps during exploration. It becomes dangerous when the category average turns into the strategic answer. Plenty of AI-generated ideas are good. My concern is that many of them are good in the same way.

A 2024 Science Advances study by Anil Doshi and Oliver Hauser examined AI assistance in short-story writing. Individual stories became more creative, especially for writers who are less naturally creative. Across the group, the stories became more similar.

The study examined short fiction, so it does not settle a design question. The tension still matters to anyone building brands. A tool can improve each option while making the whole field look more alike. The value shifts to people who can spot an answer that shouldn’t look like everyone else’s and develop it.

The hidden cost of endless options

The hardest reviews I sit in tend to have plenty of options. What they lack is agreement on what those options are meant to prove.

AI can multiply that review debt. When another route takes minutes to produce, asking for one more feels cheap. Resolving it is expensive. Senior people compare subtle variations, brand designers merge incompatible ideas, and consensus rewards whatever draws the fewest objections. More choices can postpone the responsibility to decide.

A brand is also a set of exclusions. Strategy defines who the company serves and what it promises. Creative direction gives those decisions form and rules out attractive tones, colors, and references that do not belong. Without shared criteria, preference replaces judgment. A useful direction protects a point of view from every new opinion that enters the room.

I think of good creative direction as a theory of recognition. It answers two questions: which signals should people encounter repeatedly, and why should those signals belong to this company?

The Ehrenberg-Bass Institute’s work on distinctive brand assets evaluates assets through fame and uniqueness. An element becomes valuable when people know it and link it to the right brand, not the category in general.

AI can generate a shape or a phrase in seconds. Twenty new alternatives every quarter will never make any of them famous. Distinctiveness takes discipline: choose something and keep repeating it.

What creative direction means in AI branding

In AI branding, creative direction sets the criteria for three things: what AI explores, what people select, and what the organization repeats. It connects positioning to execution, so faster production builds recognition instead of fragmenting it. The goal is a brand that stays coherent as more people produce work for it.

I see four responsibilities inside that definition.

First, establish a point of view. “We want to feel innovative” is a wish. The team needs to choose more sharply what kind of innovation the company represents. Is it precise or provocative? Quietly expert or visibly ambitious? Built for insiders, or designed to make a complex category accessible? Each answer changes the work.

Second, create productive constraints. A good constraint concentrates creativity. A limited palette, a disciplined type system, a particular photographic perspective, or a clear rule for writing claims gives the team something to push against. AI becomes more useful when the brief includes decisions, not just adjectives.

Third, select what deserves to survive. Generating is additive; directing is editorial. Someone has to tell an interesting image apart from an idea with the relevance, range, and ownership to carry a brand. That call cannot go to whichever output arrived first or collected the most votes.

Fourth, turn the selection into a system. The chosen direction must work across formats, technical messages, and everyday applications. It also has to hold when someone outside the original team picks it up a year later. A large-screen visual should stay clear as an email header, and a salesperson should be able to build a new deck from it. An identity is only as strong as its most ordinary applications.

Use AI to widen first, then narrow hard

Keeping AI to minor production tasks would miss much of its value. The practical response is to separate exploration from commitment.

I think of the sequence in four stages: framing, exploring, selecting, and systematizing. People lead the framing, because it requires understanding the business and its audience. AI accelerates exploration. People stay accountable for selection. The resulting system should make both human and AI-assisted execution more consistent.

During exploration, AI can surface references, challenge obvious metaphors, create rough compositions, and test visual territories. Abundance is productive as long as the work stays provisional. The team can move past the first idea without committing to every alternative.

Then the process has to narrow. We evaluate the strongest directions against positioning, audience, competitive context, and implementation. The key question is whether an idea is merely attractive, suitable for the category, or capable of becoming recognizably ours.

Once a direction is chosen, AI can widen again inside the system. It can adapt assets, develop campaign expressions, and test new formats. At that stage, the tool works within a brand decision instead of continually replacing it.

This sequence makes judgment visible. Teams should understand why they chose a direction, what informed it, and which rules will help it build recognition over time. Writing that reasoning down is creative work and deserves the same care.

Distinctiveness has to survive the channel

The harder test begins after approval. Can a product page, a performance ad and an operational email feel like the same company? Can a salesperson build a deck without inventing a parallel identity?

A fragile identity can produce beautiful hero images, then collapse in everyday communication. A strong one gives different teams flexibility while keeping the signals people should remember.

When in-house teams and freelance graphic designers generate assets independently, production can rise while recognition weakens. Governance should specify what can vary, what stays fixed, and who is accountable when an execution stretches the system. Leaders should ask creative partners to make those decisions usable when the original creators are not in the room.

Consistency also affects discoverability. Search engines and AI answer systems meet a brand through its website, profiles, articles, and reviews. Clear positioning and repeated language give both people and these systems a more coherent set of signals.

Asset volume measures efficiency. Brand strength shows up elsewhere. The better test is whether the work gets easier to recognize and to reproduce coherently. It should also become more firmly tied to the position the business wants to own.

The value of choosing

AI is lowering the cost of making, and that should be welcomed. It gives small teams new capabilities and experienced teams more room to explore. It also raises the value of choosing.

The brands that stand out will know which options matter. They will make those choices distinctive and repeat them until the market recognizes the result.

Creative direction is the operating logic that makes the work belong to a brand. Treating it as a human finishing touch after the machine has done the real work reverses the order.

When production becomes abundant, a brand has to protect clarity.

 ⁠

entry.title: 10 Agencies With Excellent Client Onboarding
entry.summary: Ten design agencies, studios, and independent designers share their approaches to client onboarding, from detailed discovery and clear expectations to early delivery and ongoing communication.
entry.content:
Ten design agencies, studios, and independent designers share their approaches to client onboarding, from detailed discovery and clear expectations to early delivery and ongoing communication.

A strong portfolio may get a client’s attention, but the first days of a project often determine how the rest of the relationship will work. Clear expectations, smart discovery, fast communication, and a well-defined process can make the difference between a smooth collaboration and weeks of unnecessary back-and-forth.

After reviewing agencies and studios across branding, UI/UX and web design, product design, and web and app development, we selected 10 that stood out for the way they bring new clients into a project. Some rely on detailed discovery and early strategic alignment, while others simplify onboarding, deliver something useful almost immediately, or create systems that keep everyone informed from day one.

What connects them is simple: their onboarding process gives both sides a clearer idea of what they are building, why they are building it, and what happens next.

Table of Contents

  • R Design Studio
  • Flatonica
  • Xmethod
  • Coloristy Media
  • Cozmiq – UX/UI Design Agency
  • Ivan Pokazka
  • Orbix Studio
  • Chatto (Cagatayhan)
  • 16pixel
  • DesignShare
  • What the Best Onboarding Processes Have in Common

R Design Studio

R Design Studio works across branding, web design, and digital experiences for businesses that want a stronger and more polished presence. Its portfolio includes websites for service companies, creators, and independent brands, along with visual identity work. The studio focuses on clean layouts, clear communication, and design that supports the client’s business rather than adding unnecessary complexity.

“We use a ‘Clarity Before Canvas’ approach. Before significant creative work begins, we establish what we are solving, why it matters, and how we will know the project succeeded. We then share an early creative direction and document key decisions, expectations, timelines, and feedback so clients stay involved without losing clarity.”

Flatonica

Flatonica specializes in digital products for industries such as fintech, Web3, DeFi, GameFi, dApps, and iGaming. Its work covers product design, websites, mobile apps, and frontend development. Because many of these products are technically complex, the team focuses on making interfaces easier to understand while still giving each product a strong visual identity.

“Before kickoff, we clarify the redesign goals, audience, market, competitive advantages, scope, budget, and timeline. The initial meeting then goes deeper into marketing and branding goals, success criteria, technical constraints, users, competitors, and any additional teams the project may need. We also use audits and brand-personality exercises where useful, giving us a much fuller picture before design begins.”

Xmethod

Xmethod designs and develops digital products from the early planning stage through launch. The team works on UX/UI design, web and mobile development, MVPs, and product strategy for industries such as healthcare, fintech, and Web3. Its strength lies in combining design and development, helping clients keep the product consistent from the first idea to the final build.

“Every project begins with a free presale phase where the client works with our product owner, business analyst, design lead, project manager, and tech lead before committing financially. Together, we map user flows and create an initial design concept, then move into a paid analysis phase if the fit is right. It lets clients see how we think before making a larger commitment.”

Coloristy Media

Coloristy Media combines UX/UI design, web design, and branding for digital companies. Its work includes SaaS, fintech, AI, healthtech, B2B platforms, dashboards, and websites. The agency is especially well suited to products with complex information, where the main challenge is making the experience easier to understand without losing the personality of the brand.

“We avoid generic intake forms. Instead, we find a reference website or brand the client already relates to, break it into specific components, and build questions around those examples. Once the project starts, clients also receive an onboarding package showing what we need from them, due dates, responsibilities, and who is handling each part on our side.”

Cozmiq – UX/UI Design Agency

Cozmiq provides ongoing design support for startups and growing companies. The studio works on SaaS products, dashboards, websites, landing pages, and other UX/UI needs across industries such as fintech, healthcare, logistics, and consumer apps. Its subscription model is designed for teams that need regular access to product and web design without building a large internal design department.

“Our onboarding starts with a structured discovery form followed by a kickoff call. We use those steps to align on business goals, target users, scope, deliverables, timeline, and approvals before sharing a project roadmap with milestones and next steps. It cuts down on unnecessary back-and-forth and scope confusion.”

Ivan Pokazka

Ivan Pokazka works on web, mobile, and product design, with a strong focus on information-dense interfaces. His portfolio includes SaaS products, trading platforms, gaming products, and digital asset tools. Much of the work centers on dashboards, responsive interfaces, and product systems that need to stay clear even when the underlying product is complex.

“Every project starts with an intake form that asks about business goals, what is broken today, and what went wrong with previous freelancers or agencies. That last question tells me which expectations need to be addressed immediately. I also establish a 48-hour feedback window and use Loom walkthroughs so clients understand the reasoning behind decisions and know exactly what happens next.”

Orbix Studio

Orbix Studio focuses on UX/UI design for complex enterprise software. The agency works on dashboards, internal tools, customer platforms, design systems, accessibility, and frontend development. Its work is particularly relevant for companies with large or growing products that need clearer structure, better usability, and a design system that can support new features over time.

“As for our onboarding approach, we swear by a “Project Discovery Questionnaire” that we send clients before our kickoff call. It helps us understand their goals and pain points beforehand, allowing us to hit the ground running during the meeting and ensure we’re immediately focused on the most critical tasks.”

Chatto (Cagatayhan)

Chatto works on digital products and websites for startups and technology companies in areas such as AI, SaaS, Web3, fintech, ecommerce, and B2B. His work includes mobile apps, dashboards, marketing websites, branding, design systems, and Framer builds. A common focus across these projects is making technical products easier to understand and easier to use.

“Our main onboarding principle is removing ambiguity early. Before starting, we align on goals, scope, deliverables, timelines, communication channels, and success metrics. We also use asynchronous updates and Loom recordings so clients can stay informed without filling their calendars with meetings.”

16pixel

16pixel designs digital products for web and mobile, including SaaS platforms, AI products, dashboards, and apps. The studio has worked across healthcare, finance, ecommerce, and technology, supporting startups and larger companies. Its portfolio combines modern interface design with practical product thinking, especially for products that need to turn complex features into a simple user experience.

“Before we design a screen, we align on the product, business goals, users, and success metrics. A kickoff workshop helps us map priorities, agree on scope, and establish communication from day one. That shared understanding reduces revisions and keeps the project moving around the same set of goals.”

DesignShare

DesignShare focuses on practical product design for B2B software. The team works on dashboards, admin panels, onboarding flows, settings, permissions, tables, design systems, and other parts of a product that users rely on every day. It also offers ongoing design support for companies that need regular UX/UI, Webflow, or Framer work without hiring a full in-house team.

“We removed onboarding as a separate phase. Once a client subscribes, their project manager gets in touch quickly and the first request can enter the queue the same day. We learn the client’s preferences through feedback on real work, while one project manager remains the single point of contact so the client never has to repeat the same brief to multiple people.”

What the Best Onboarding Processes Have in Common

The agencies on this list take different approaches, but the strongest processes all reduce uncertainty early. Some do that through detailed discovery, others through faster delivery, shared workspaces, early concepts, or clear communication rules.

For clients, onboarding is also a useful preview of the working relationship ahead. A clear process at the start usually makes scope, feedback, responsibilities, and next steps easier to manage throughout the project.

entry.title: B2B Website Design in Webflow: What Matters After Launch
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and The Branded Agency Head of Brand and Growth Quincy Samycia shares how Webflow design systems free B2B marketing teams from constant agency dependence.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and The Branded Agency Head of Brand and Growth Quincy Samycia shares how Webflow design systems free B2B marketing teams from constant agency dependence.

About the Author:
Quincy Samycia is Head of Brand and Growth at The Branded Agency, a branding, creative, website and growth agency working with ambitious companies across Canada, the United States and international markets. He helps organizations connect brand strategy with the creative, digital experiences and marketing systems responsible for measurable growth.

The promise of building a website in an afternoon is easy to appreciate when you run a business. There is always something waiting to be launched, explained or improved, and rarely enough time to give it the attention it deserves. A tool that lets a small team make progress without a lengthy production cycle is worth taking seriously.

I say that as someone who co-founded an agency. I have an obvious interest in the future of creative work, and I think our industry should welcome the pressure to explain its value. Clients are entitled to ask why they should pay for something technology has made easier. “This is how we’ve always done it” is a poor answer.

My reservation is about what we consider finished.

A convincing first version can be valuable. It can help a founder express an idea, give a marketing team something concrete to debate, or get a modest campaign into the market. For some businesses, that may be enough. I would be reluctant to turn a straightforward requirement into an elaborate agency engagement simply because we know how to deliver one.

Why B2B websites need to keep evolving

An established B2B company has a different set of demands. Its website has to represent a business that keeps changing, often through decisions made by people with different priorities. The person approving the brand expression may have little involvement in product claims. The sales team may need evidence that marketing has not yet collected. A technical expert may be the only person qualified to approve a sentence that everyone else thinks sounds perfectly reasonable.

These are ordinary business realities. They tend to become visible just after the launch everyone worked so hard to achieve.

Product marketing needs a page for a new solution. Sales wants a customer story relevant to an unfamiliar industry. The leadership team has refined the company’s position. A campaign deadline is approaching, and the people responsible for the website are trying to accommodate all of it without undoing the work they just approved.

That is where I would start judging the investment. Can the company respond confidently? Does the website make the next decision easier, or does each request reopen the entire project?

The next hundred changes are a useful way to think about it. Some will be trivial. Others will reveal whether the business bought a coherent system or a collection of pages that happened to look coherent on launch day.

A Webflow design system should leave room for change

I care about that distinction because good design is valuable precisely when it survives contact with real business needs. A longer headline should not wreck the hierarchy. A technical diagram should have a considered place to live. A page for an engineering evaluator may need more explanation than a page for a finance leader. Both should feel unmistakably like the same company.

Giving a marketing team that flexibility takes judgment. Too little structure creates inconsistency; too much makes every new idea a struggle. There is a point at which protecting the design becomes protecting it from the people it was supposed to help.

That balance is one of the reasons I find Webflow useful. It gives Webflow designers and developers a way to establish a visual system that other people can work within. The quality of the result depends heavily on how that system is designed, how its content is organized, and whether the people inheriting it understand the choices available to them.

A platform can provide the means to work well. The company and its partners still have to decide how they will use them.

Consider a customer story. Publishing it is a relatively small task. Making it useful across the business takes more thought: which industry it belongs to, which product claims it supports, where a prospect should encounter it, and whether sales can find it when a relevant question arises. The most useful development work may be the part that saves someone from making those connections manually every time.

There is a similar judgment involved in deciding what a team should be able to change on its own. Routine publishing should be routine. A new integration, a substantial change to the brand, or a more complex interactive experience may warrant specialist involvement. Independence works best when people understand both their freedom and its limits.

Furiosa’s Webflow migration and the value of a good handoff

Our website design and development work with Furiosa, an AI infrastructure company, is a good illustration. The brief was to migrate its existing website from Craft CMS to Webflow, preserving the experience while creating a more manageable foundation.

We rebuilt the design in Figma, developed a style guide and reusable components, and organized the Webflow CMS for blog posts, careers and newsroom content. The site then went through testing across pages, components and screen sizes. We also delivered three training sessions covering Webflow fundamentals, CMS management and ongoing maintenance.

I think the training deserves attention in that story. It is easy to admire a finished page and overlook what someone needs to know to maintain it six months later. The ambition should be a client team that can use what has been built and knows where to turn when its requirements change.

That raises an uncomfortable question for agencies: how much of the dependence we create is actually necessary?

There will always be work that benefits from specialist expertise. But if a client needs us for every routine edit because the structure is confusing or the handoff was inadequate, I would struggle to describe that as a successful relationship. A strong partnership should make the client more capable. There is plenty of worthwhile work beyond being the only person who knows how the website functions.

AI makes web design faster. Judgment still matters.

AI gives this question more urgency. At The Branded Agency, we use it to support efficient production, and I want clients to benefit from that progress. Faster exploration can give us more room to refine an idea. Less repetitive work can give experienced web designers more time to resolve the difficult parts. Those are practical improvements, provided someone remains responsible for the quality of what leaves the studio.

Creative direction still matters. Some clients have a clear vision and need help realizing it accurately. Others know their current presentation feels wrong but cannot yet describe what would feel right. Generating more options can help either conversation, although it can also prolong a decision when nobody has established what makes one option appropriate.

For me, the human contribution includes listening closely enough to distinguish those situations. It means being able to explain why a design choice serves the business, recognizing when an attractive idea misrepresents the product, and knowing when a client’s hesitation is telling us something we have missed. That work requires attention even when the tools become faster.

Webflow’s recent product announcements are interesting in this context. Its builder updates at Webflow Conf 2026 included visual editing for AI code components and reusable components within CMS rich text. It also introduced Source by Webflow, announced as a limited research preview connecting code, marketing tools and work by people and AI agents.

What interests me about that direction is the prospect of giving more people useful control over the work. I am less persuaded by a demonstration of speed alone. I want to know whether a team can understand the result, refine it and maintain it. The distinction between a capability available today and a product in preview also matters when a business is making a commitment.

Website bottlenecks often start inside the business

There is another side to this that an agency should be honest about. Sometimes the website is waiting on the company.

A campaign can be ready to publish while several stakeholders debate the message. A product page can remain outdated because nobody is responsible for confirming the information. A new tool may remove production work without changing either situation. Leadership still has to decide who owns the decision and how much review it reasonably needs.

This is why I am cautious about treating every slow website process as a technology problem. It might be a poorly built system. It might be an overcomplicated approval process. It might be a perfectly sensible pause to check something that matters. Knowing the difference is part of running the business.

For a company selling complex products or services, the stakes extend beyond publication speed. The website may help a prospect understand an unfamiliar offer, give an internal champion something useful to share, or answer a question that would otherwise delay a sales conversation. A team needs enough control to keep that information relevant and enough discipline to keep it trustworthy.

The everyday work that makes a website valuable

A beautiful launch is worth celebrating. So is the quieter achievement of a marketing team publishing good work without a crisis, a salesperson finding the right evidence, or a new employee understanding how the website is meant to operate.

When I think about the value of a website, I think about those ordinary working days. The business will change its mind, learn something about its customers and pursue an opportunity nobody anticipated in the original brief. Good creative and technical work should leave it better equipped to do that.

AI makes me optimistic about how much easier parts of this work can become. It also makes me more demanding about the choices we make with the time we gain. The next hundred changes will give us a much better answer about the quality of a website than launch day ever could.

entry.title: Our Winning Strategy for FIFA World Cup 2026 NYNJ Website Design
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and DD.NYC® Creative Director Anjelika Lours' Kour reveals the collaborative strategy behind the official FIFA World Cup 26 NYNJ website, balancing award-worthy design with utilitarian performance to represent the region on a global stage.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and DD.NYC® Creative Director Anjelika Lours' Kour reveals the collaborative strategy behind the official FIFA World Cup 26 NYNJ website, balancing award-worthy design with utilitarian performance to represent the region on a global stage.

About the Author:
DD.NYC® Creative Director & Managing Partner Anjelika Lours’ Kour specializes in corporate branding, web design, and video storytelling. Beyond working with powerhouse clients, she actively shapes the wider creative industry as a global judge for the International Academy of Digital Arts and Sciences (IADAS) and the Scholastic Art & Writing Awards.

We were tasked to build the FIFA World Cup 2026™ NYNJ official website in time for the world’s biggest sporting event, back in the US for the first time since ‘94. 

DD.NYC® became the Digital Agency of Record for the Host Committee, which meant the site wasn’t a marketing add-on. It was the front door where fans, sponsors, media, and partners from every part of the world would go to understand what this region was bringing to the tournament.

The brief had a built-in tension we knew we’d be working against from day one. The site had to feel unmistakably global, because billions of people were going to see it, and unmistakably local, because it represented one specific region and had to earn its place next to every other host city in the world. 

I’ll give you an overview of how our web designers approached the project and what became our winning strategy. 

Making a sports website award-worthy and utilitarian

We needed the site to be two things: award-worthy and utilitarian. But they don’t always result from the same process. 

Award-worthy, because a project this visible was always going to be judged against the best design work in the world, apart from other sports websites. 

Utilitarian, because it had to perform. Mobile-first, fast under real traffic, legible across languages and devices, built for an audience that would be arriving from everywhere at once.

Those two goals pull in different directions. Bold, ownable design decisions can slow a site down or complicate a build. A build optimized purely for speed and scale can end up looking generic. 

Then there was the scale of who we were working with. FIFA and a Host Committee aren’t a typical client relationship. There are more stakeholders, approval layers, and a brand system that has to answer to an organization operating at a global level. That kind of structure changes the rhythm of a project before a single pixel gets designed.

All of that is part of why this became one of the most demanding projects we’ve taken on as an agency. By the time we wrapped, we’d put in roughly a multiple of hours we’d typically spend on a project of this type. It’s a clear marker of how much the scope and complexity grew once we were fully inside it.

Design teams brought together by one goal

Instead of assigning to a chosen few, we opened it up to our entire design staff. Anyone who wanted to contribute to something this high-profile could put their hand up and get involved, rather than the work being routed to a small, fixed pod the way most projects are staffed. 

For a milestone project landing in our 10th year as an agency, that felt like the right call. This was the kind of work our whole team should get to be part of, not just a handful of people.

That approach also matched the nature of the brief. A project asking us to represent an entire region, for an audience of billions, benefited from more perspectives in the room. It meant more ideas got tested, more instincts got compared against each other, and the final direction had been stress-tested by a wider group before it ever reached the client.

The other deliberate choice was to let history do some of the design work. Rather than building the visual system from a blank page, the team went back and looked at how past World Cups and host cities had approached their own identity and design language. 

That research became part of the foundation. Something we used to understand what had worked, what had felt dated fast, and where there was room to do something the tournament hadn’t quite seen from a host city before. 

The result merges FIFA’s global brand language with the identity of the New York/New Jersey region, built mobile-first from the ground up to handle real-world scale.

Celebrating wins and milestones

The site launched as a mobile-first build designed to hold up under serious global traffic, with a design system built to carry FIFA’s global brand alongside the region’s own identity across every device and screen size. 

Since launch, it’s been recognized across the digital design community: an Awwwards Honorable Mention, a Special Kudos from CSS Design Awards, and a feature in the One Page Love Inspiration Collection. It also picked up wins in the Q3 2025 Online Design Awards Competition, including a Studio/Agency win in Brand Collateral and a Gold in Website Design.

We’re thankful for the recognition but more so on what the project meant to us. It landed in our first decade as an agency, and it’s the kind of project that tests whether everything you’ve built actually holds up when the stakes are this visible. 

Opening the work to the whole team, going back into design history instead of skipping it, and being honest with ourselves about how much time a project like this actually takes were the choices that got us there, more than any single design decision on the page.

entry.title: Before You Rebrand: How a Brand Audit Reveals What Actually Needs to Change
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and The Branded Agency Head of Brand and Growth Quincy Samycia explains how to distinguish positioning, messaging, execution and identity issues before commissioning a rebrand.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and The Branded Agency Head of Brand and Growth Quincy Samycia explains how to distinguish positioning, messaging, execution and identity issues before commissioning a rebrand.

About the Author:
Quincy Samycia is Head of Brand and Growth at The Branded Agency, a branding, creative, website and growth agency working with ambitious companies across Canada, the United States and international markets. He helps organizations connect brand strategy with the creative, digital experiences and marketing systems responsible for measurable growth.

Before rebranding, conduct a brand audit to determine whether the problem is positioning, messaging, inconsistent execution, customer experience, or identity. A full rebrand becomes more defensible when the existing brand prevents the business from expressing a credible strategic direction.

A dated website, an unclear sales story, or a weaker campaign response can trigger a rebrand conversation. These observations describe discomfort, not its cause.

Moving directly to design risks replacing familiar assets without resolving the underlying problem. First establish what is broken, what still has value, and what customers already recognize.

“We need a rebrand” usually describes a symptom

A founder may mean the company has outgrown its market. Sales may mean prospects misunderstand the offer. Marketing may mean channels use conflicting assets. Customers may mean the experience doesn’t justify the price.

Each needs a different response. New visuals can’t differentiate an undifferentiated offer, fix a confusing checkout, or create ownership of brand guidelines. So the first job is working out which change the business can justify.

A brand audit separates symptoms from causes

A brand audit is a structured review of the gap between the brand a company intends to create and the brand people actually encounter. It compares strategy, language, identity, experience, and perception to produce evidence for decisions, including what to preserve and what to improve. It has five layers:

1. Internal intent. Agree on the priority audience, business direction, and credible advantages. If leaders disagree, the identity is being asked to express a strategy that hasn’t been resolved.

2. Public expression. Review the website, social profiles, ads, sales materials, recruitment communications, and support experience. Look at what’s in circulation today, not just the launch guidelines.

3. Market perception. Compare internal assumptions with customer interviews, reviews, sales conversations, employee feedback, and support questions. Find the gaps between the meaning you intended and what people actually understand.

4. Competitive context. Compare promises, visual conventions, and category language. Consistency gives little advantage if your story is interchangeable with your competitors’.

5. Experience and evidence. Check whether the experience proves the promise. Simplicity requires an easy buying journey, expertise needs evidence, and premium positioning needs credible service and delivery.

Four different problems are commonly mistaken for one rebrand problem

Classify the findings before setting the creative scope.

1. A positioning problem. The company can’t explain who it serves, what value it offers, or why customers should choose it. Generic homepage claims and inconsistent sales explanations are common symptoms. Research the audience and market, identify credible differentiation, and make strategic choices before redesigning.

2. A messaging problem. The strategy is sound, but internal terminology obscures the value or proof arrives too late. Rebuild the value proposition, message hierarchy, voice, and audience-specific language.

3. An execution and governance problem. A useful identity has fragmented: outdated logos circulate, campaigns invent their own styles, and sales materials contradict the website. Consolidate assets, improve templates, clarify approval rules, and assign ownership. Better governance may be the answer, not a new identity.

4. A genuine identity problem. The name or identity creates the wrong category expectation, undermines credibility, or can’t support the business’s direction. A merger, a new market, or a changed business model can expose these limits. The test is strategic usefulness, not whether the identity feels old.

The evidence should determine the scope

A rebranding strategy should connect each finding to the right response: reposition, rewrite, systematize, redesign, or a combination. The audit diagnoses the problem. A rebrand changes the strategy or identity when that diagnosis supports it.

If the experience contradicts the promise, fix the experience. Communication can’t hide that gap indefinitely.

Protect existing brand equity: recognition, search demand, familiar language, and trusted associations. Record what deserves to stay alongside what needs to change, then choose the project that closes the most important gap with the least unnecessary disruption.

AI search has turned brand consistency into a visibility issue

Search engines and AI assistants encounter websites, profiles, reviews, listings, and third-party references. They infer the company’s identity from those public sources.

Coherent names, categories, audiences, expertise, and proof make that identity easier to interpret. Conflicting descriptions can produce ambiguity. An “enterprise consultancy” on the homepage, a “creative studio” on LinkedIn, and a “software provider” in directories present three different expectations.

Audit facts and positioning across sources while letting language adapt to context. Support important claims with credible evidence. Consistency can improve interpretability, though it doesn’t guarantee rankings or AI citations.

Can a brand audit improve SEO, AEO, and GEO?

It can identify contradictory company information, unclear expertise, and missing proof. Addressing those gaps supports machine understanding without guaranteeing visibility.

Mini case study: humanizing data inside PepsiCo

Our work with PepsiCo’s Data Science & Advanced Analytics team could have been framed as visual modernization. The diagnosis showed a perception problem. The team powered insights across major brands, yet data science could feel technical and intimidating to internal stakeholders, and potential recruits could miss its role in shaping global commerce.

We repositioned the story around what data enabled: clearer foresight, better decisions, and greater confidence. The identity balanced precision with warmth across messaging, presentations, internal communications, recruitment materials, and the team’s app. The gaps in strategy and communication defined the visual system’s job. Without diagnosis, the team might have received a polished version of the same inaccessible story.

View the PepsiCo Labs Data Science and Advanced Analytics case study

When a full rebrand is actually justified

There’s no universal threshold, but the case gets stronger when:

  • The business or category has changed substantially
  • A merger requires new brand architecture
  • The name limits growth
  • Priority audiences no longer recognize themselves
  • Research shows the identity reduces trust
  • The visual system lacks the range needed across products, markets, and digital experiences

One issue may justify an update. Several connected constraints can support broader change.

Identify what must survive, whether a name, color, symbol, phrase, or product story. Continuity protects useful memory, and a clearer system can feel new without erasing every recognizable asset.

How do you know whether your company needs a rebrand?

Look for evidence that the identity or name blocks the business’s direction. Messaging or governance problems may need narrower changes.

Run the audit before writing the creative brief

Use the audit to define the audience, business change, perception gap, assets to retain, required evidence, and the observable job of the new system.

Start with current touchpoints and competitor materials. Compare claims, language, identity, and proof, and ask customers and employees how they describe the company. Note confusion, friction, and overlooked strengths.

Teams that want an outside-in starting point can review public brand, website, search, reputation, and AI-visibility signals and turn them into a prioritized diagnostic, as in The Branded Agency’s Brand Health Audit. This doesn’t replace customer interviews or a full strategic engagement, but it can show where deeper investigation is most likely to matter.

Translate findings into decisions with priorities and owners, rather than delivering observations alone. Brand designers can then carry those decisions into the identity and system.

How often should you conduct a brand audit?

Consider an annual review, plus additional checks before expansion, mergers, website redesigns, or major audience changes.

A good audit should make the answer smaller and clearer

The answer may be a new identity, clearer positioning, stronger proof, or templates people can use. A company shouldn’t replace its whole brand to solve every brand problem.

We audit first, preserve useful recognition, and change only what keeps the company from being easier to understand, trust, and choose.

entry.title: Why Website Redesigns Fail Before the First Screen Is Designed
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and The Branded Agency Head of Brand and Growth Quincy Samycia explains why strong redesigns begin with positioning, decision architecture, proof and measurement before the first screen is designed.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and The Branded Agency Head of Brand and Growth Quincy Samycia explains why strong redesigns begin with positioning, decision architecture, proof and measurement before the first screen is designed.

About the Author:
Quincy Samycia is Head of Brand and Growth at The Branded Agency, a branding, creative, website and growth agency working with ambitious companies across Canada, the United States and international markets. He helps organizations connect brand strategy with the creative, digital experiences and marketing systems responsible for measurable growth.

Website redesigns fail when teams change the interface before they settle on audience priorities, positioning, content, customer journeys and measures of success. A strong website redesign strategy defines those foundations first, then uses UX/UI design, development and testing to turn them into a clearer, more useful experience.

A dated interface, crowded navigation and slow publishing are symptoms. At The Branded Agency, our website strategy, UX/UI design and development work starts with a different question: what decision should this website help the right person make?

That question shifts the conversation from preference to purpose. It makes us define the audience, the value of the offer, the evidence needed to believe it and the path from interest to action. It also shows that many apparent design problems are unresolved business, brand or content problems.

A website redesign brief usually describes symptoms

“Make it modern” may signal outdated positioning. “Simplify it” may point to an undefined priority audience. “Improve conversion” may mean the offer lacks proof. “Make it easier to update” may mean no one owns the content.

Moving to Webflow or Shopify doesn’t answer any of those questions. Platform requirements should come out of the diagnosis, not stand in for it. When we skip that step, design inherits decisions the business has avoided, and the result is a polished website that is still hard to understand.

Brand, decision and operations: the three jobs of a website

We treat a website as three connected systems:

  • Brand: makes the company recognizable and communicates a distinct point of view.
  • Decision: helps visitors judge relevance, credibility and the next step.
  • Operations: lets marketing publish, sales share useful destinations and internal teams keep content accurate.

When one system dominates, the trade-offs are predictable: memorable but vague storytelling, interchangeable conversion tactics, or efficient but uninspiring templates. Our goal is a website strategy that links expression, action and operation in one customer experience.

Six questions every website redesign should answer

Before we sketch a wireframe, we want clear answers to these questions:

  • Who is the priority audience?
  • What are they trying to accomplish?
  • What makes this offer meaningfully different?
  • What must they understand before they can act?
  • What proof will reduce their doubt?
  • Which action represents real business value?

Vague answers produce generic hero copy, navigation organized by department and competing calls to action. That is why we let positioning and messaging shape the sitemap: they decide what matters, in what order and to whom.

The website redesign process

When copywriters fill predetermined boxes and analytics arrives near launch, teams lose the chance to shape the experience. We start the website redesign process by mapping the visitor’s decision.

  1. Start from where the visitor is
    Visitors may be researching a category, comparing options, validating a recommendation or getting ready to buy, and each stage needs a different path. Someone arriving from a specific campaign may need product evidence right away, while someone researching the category may need context first. The content sequence should account for those entry points.
  2. Name the decision they are trying to make
    Vague goals such as ‘learn more’ become a concrete question: does this product fit my workflow? Can I justify its price? The page is then built around the answer.
  3. Sequence claim, meaning and proof
    “Faster” invites “compared with what?” “Trusted” invites “by whom?” We explain what each benefit means and place supporting evidence next to the claim.
  4. Remove friction and keep the character
    Clarity depends on hierarchy. Cutting words or colours alone rarely achieves it. We keep the next step visible and preserve a distinctive voice and visual identity. Then we test whether someone can identify the offer, find relevant evidence and locate the next step without help from the project team. If they can’t, revisit sequence and emphasis before adding content or stripping back the identity.
  5. Define success before choosing the solution
    We define the intended outcome before selecting platforms, components and analytics. What success looks like depends on the business: an enterprise site may prioritize publishing workflows, an eCommerce site may need strong product discovery, and a lead generation site may need qualification and sales follow-up. We choose Webflow, Shopify or another platform against those requirements, not the other way around.

Proof should be part of the design system

Proof belongs where visitors encounter doubt, not on a disconnected testimonial page. We match the evidence to the claim:

  • Performance: benchmarks, results or demonstrations.
  • Expertise: relevant case studies, credentials or process.
  • Trust: reviews, recognizable clients and transparent policies.
  • Usability: an experience that is easy to complete.
  • Brand: consistency between the promise and the experience.

We map proof during wireframing because evidence changes layouts and content requirements. Sometimes an unsupported claim has to change as well.

Build a content system, not a collection of pages

A refined homepage must eventually support dozens of less prominent pages, and reusable components alone won’t make that system scale.

A content system defines page purposes, field relationships, content limits, reusable proof patterns and rules for variation. Ownership is assigned so teams know who creates, approves and maintains content, and each element is marked as mandatory or optional, with a clear link between proof and products or services. A content model should reflect how the organization actually creates and updates information.

Whether you hire Webflow designers or Shopify designers, make sure templates are tested with real content and with the people who will publish it.

Flexibility should support informed choices without breaking hierarchy. The best handoff isn’t a library of blocks; it’s a set of choices the internal team can make with confidence.

What this looked like for Milton Coffee Co.

Milton Coffee Co. came to us with a specific eCommerce website redesign problem: the site did not communicate the value of its premium, customizable coffee machines clearly enough.

We began with discovery and creative exploration, kept the existing branding and photography, and refined the homepage and section copy. A customized Shopify template, dynamic product templates and a third-party “design your own” integration supported the buying journey.

Behind the screen, the templates also simplified future product uploads. The work connected what customers needed to understand with what the internal team needed to maintain, which took the project beyond a visual refresh.

Performance and accessibility are design requirements

We treat speed, stability, responsiveness and accessibility as design inputs from the start of the project.

Google’s Core Web Vitals guidance focuses on loading performance, interactivity and visual stability, because these are measurable parts of the experience real users receive. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are organized around content being perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.

In practice, that means budgeting for media and animation, protecting contrast, using meaningful headings and supporting keyboard interaction. These decisions affect both comprehension and usability. A website that promises simplicity but loads slowly or excludes visitors contradicts its own message.

Treat launch as the start of learning

Launch begins observation of the complete website; it doesn’t end the redesign. Prototype testing reduces risk, but real behaviour will still raise questions the project team didn’t anticipate. The Nielsen Norman Group’s iterative homepage redesign case study is a useful illustration of design improving through rounds of prototyping, testing and refinement rather than a single reveal.

We set baseline measures before launch, then review:

  • Can priority visitors find the information they need?
  • Which messages and proof encourage useful action?
  • Where do qualified visitors hesitate or leave?
  • Can the team publish without weakening the system?

The answers set improvement priorities. Qualified inquiries, completed purchases and publishing efficiency deserve a look alongside conversion rate, since not every click carries equal weight.

Settle the foundations before you approve a mockup

Before approving a mockup, confirm the audience, positioning, offer, proof, content model and success measures, and include performance, accessibility and measurement in the brief.

A successful website redesign makes the business easier to understand, the next decision easier to make and the system easier to improve. Those outcomes begin with choices made before the first screen.

entry.title: 7 Ways To Close The Gap Between AI-Generated Apps and Great Product Design
entry.summary: Dribbble Community Leader and Expo Product & Brand Designer Nicolas Solerieu talks about closing the gap between AI-generated apps and great product design, from replacing default icons to designing for error states and edge cases AI tends to skip.
entry.content:
Dribbble Community Leader and Expo Product & Brand Designer Nicolas Solerieu talks about closing the gap between AI-generated apps and great product design, from replacing default icons to designing for error states and edge cases AI tends to skip.

About the Author:
Nicolas Solerieu is a product and brand designer at Expo, working across product, web, and brand identity. Previously at GitHub and Opendoor, he’s interested in software, the web, and the strange craft of arranging rectangles for a living.

You can’t one-shot an app. The capabilities are on the table, and mature frameworks and skilled LLMs are within reach. Chances are you’ve used vibe-coded software, and noticed differences. The obvious flaws are disappearing. What remains is subtler: the gap between an AI-generated app that works and one that feels considered.

1. Build a Brand System for Your AI-Generated App

Good product design blurs the edges between brand and product. Ask an LLM, even in plan mode, and it will improvise a branding kit to suit its own needs. Even in tools like Claude Design, where you can provide a base kit, it will still create brand artifacts of its own. Illustration should be consistent, and colors and layout should create a visual continuity from marketing to product, guiding users along the way.

The various touchpoints require different fidelity. Marketing is usually higher fidelity while products tend to be more minimal and rely on color and icons alone. Infusing a product with personality and a distinct style is almost an art. It requires care, attention, and taste: human qualities that can only be amplified, not outsourced.

A brand is also a living entity that flexes beyond the system an AI can understand: employee swag, micro events, an internal sports team, fan art. These are where a product’s personality shows up in ways no brand kit specifies. Think of a brand as the set of artifacts that breathes life into your product. A simple motto is a good way to keep this in mind: “small screens, big moments.”

2. Replace Default Icons and Generic AI Illustrations

Most LLMs pull icons out of their preferred library, or invent them with SVG and CSS. Without specific direction, the result is often generic. 90% of the apps I saw use Lucide icons. It’s solid and covers most cases, but at this scale, it’s becoming the obvious default. You can do better and easily. The same goes for illustration. Certain styles and obvious quality flaws can erode trust quickly.

3. Use Purposeful, Restrained Animation in Your App UI

LLMs greatly ease the production of animation. They tend to go hard on the same attributes since CSS and SVG make them most accessible, and shaders are also more prominent nowadays. The downside is that interfaces can accumulate motion before anyone has asked for it. It happens to me all the time with all my frontend design skills loaded up by default. Animation is rarely improved by quantity. More often than not, restraint and purpose are needed on the human side to improve the quality of outcomes.

4. Test on Real Devices to Make Your Mobile App Feel Native

You may have noticed a strong enthusiasm for products that “feel native.” This feeling often boils down to performance and familiarity. Design is the experience, and ease and speed are a big part of it. Only a human can truly feel that quality, so test, test and test again. Your firsthand experience with each ecosystem matters.

Simulators help here, too. When an agent can launch your app in a simulator, tap through flows, and test what it built, a typically painful part of the process becomes visual and collaborative. You can watch it work, spot what feels off, and steer it in real time. It speeds up the loop, but it doesn’t replace the device in your hand, so keep testing on real hardware before you call it done.

5. Enforce Design System Consistency and Visual Hierarchy

All of the above is well and good, but what often betrays a UX is inconsistency across the whole UI. LLMs are getting better at sticking to a design system, but as anyone who has worked in this industry knows, having a design system guarantees nothing. The wrong component or primitive still ends up in the wrong place. Systems are flexible, and LLMs will be only as flawed as humans.

That’s why the visual basics still need a human eye. LLMs are getting better at checking them, but human taste remains the best judge. Great visual design guides the eye so information feels effortless to digest. Contrast and visual hierarchy make the most important details pop first. Alignment and proximity keep related pieces grouped so the layout feels orderly rather than chaotic. Whitespace gives elements room to breathe, creating a balanced design that feels clean, clear, and intentional.

6. Plan Migrations and Involve Users and Partners Before You Prompt

Design sits at the intersection of operations, engineering, marketing, and infrastructure. Great design is often the direct product of a purposeful blend of those priorities, and that’s hard to convey to LLMs, which either wait for precise instruction or take (sometimes wild) guesses. 

Some scenarios, like migrations, are more straightforward. Others require more planning and handholding. Porting over your web app to mobile? Going native? These can seem like perfect tasks for AI but often result in many edge cases. Careful review via simulators and platform knowledge goes a long way. It’s never just a design matter. I’d encourage you to think about the contingencies and holistic drivers.

The same goes for the people involved. You might have heard “don’t ship your org chart.” While a great app is a set of features, UX is the sum of all things, too many things to truly list in one blog post. Points of friction, and human shortcomings often materialize in the experience. Talking to your users, and your relationships with project partners and vendors, are an invisible yet obvious part of the design process that LLMs can’t fully replace. Sometimes they even introduce a new kind of friction.

7. Design for Error States, Empty States, and Accessibility, Not Just the Happy Path

The modern product designer is not someone who starts from a blank canvas but an “Editor-in-Chief” who curates, prunes, and directs AI outputs. More like a webmaster of the 2000s than a 2016 product designer. Steering and QC is more important than ever to avoid the “Happy Path” Trap: LLMs excel at ideal user flows, but product design happens in the margins. AI frequently ignores error states, zero-data screens, dynamic text wrapping, role-based views, focus & accessibility requirements, loading indicators, and all too often, container alignment. Brand remains the wild west, and it should. That’s where the beautiful complexity of design shows.

Polish is when persistence and taste meet the craft of design. AI elevates the floor so anyone can build software, and human craft is what raises the ceiling. Since tools are becoming generalists, perhaps designers need to become generalists (again) too.
